title: Pressure, inclination, heaviness and lightness (*iʿtimād*, *mayl*)
en:
### Pressure, inclination, heaviness and lightness (*iʿtimād*, *mayl*)

**Second investigation.** The term **iʿtimād** can mean the **sensible resistance or pressure** exerted by a body against something preventing it from moving in a given direction. So understood, it is a tangible quality. Its existence and its distinction both from **motion** and from the body's **nature** are clear. It can be felt where there is no motion, as with a stone held suspended in the air or an inflated waterskin held below the water's surface. It can also be absent although the body's nature persists, as when a body rests in its natural place. Alternatively, *iʿtimād* can mean the **principle of that resistance**, defined as the quality by which a body presses against an obstacle to movement in a given direction. The existence of this principle and its difference from nature will be established later; what remains uncertain is **which class of quality** it belongs to.

**On the words, “And its kinds may be made.”** Some enumerate six kinds of inclination in respect of movement in the six spatial directions. They may call all six mutually contrary if **maximum opposition** is not required for contrariety; if maximum opposition is required, contrariety holds only between opposite directions, such as upward and downward. The division into six genuine species is weak for two reasons.

First, natural inclinations that can really differ in quiddity are only **ascending and descending inclination**, toward above and below. These are the two directions whose reality does not change. An upside-down person has not made below into above: his feet now point above and his head below. The other directions are relational. Someone who previously faced east and now faces west has made his former front the rear and his right the left, and conversely. The supposed pressures directed forward, backward, rightward and leftward are renamed by a shift in orientation; they cannot therefore constitute different species of a single physical quality.

Second, the reduction of directions to six is **conventional**. Ordinary people derive it from the human body's head, feet, back, belly and two hands; technical investigators derive it from three dimensions intersecting at right angles, each with two ends. In reality the possible directions are numerous: as many as the atomic parts on the theory of indivisible atoms, or indefinitely many according to the possible divisions admitted by those who reject such atoms. The two genuine and invariant species are therefore **weight** and **lightness**, namely the downward and upward tendencies.

Each occurs absolutely or relatively. **Absolute heaviness** is a quality that moves a body until its **centre of gravity**—the point around which the material on all sides is balanced—coincides with the centre of the universe, as earth is said to do. **Relative heaviness** is a quality moving a body toward the centre across most of the interval from circumference to centre, but without reaching the centre, as in water: water is heavy relative to fire and air, but not relative to earth. **Absolute lightness** is a quality impelling the body outward until its surface coincides with the inner surface of the lunar sphere, as fire was held to do. **Relative lightness** impels a body outward across most of the interval but does not reach the encompassing boundary, as in air.

**On the words, “And they do not reduce to...”** The majority maintain that heaviness and lightness are additional bodily qualities which cannot be reduced to moisture and dryness. Air is light although moist, while earth is heavy although dry. Al-Jubbāʾī says, instead, that **moisture causes heaviness** and **dryness causes lightness**, pointing to moisture in heavy things such as gold and the way lighter materials such as wood turn to ash when burned. **Reply:** this at most shows moisture and dryness occurring in *some* things that are heavy and light. It does not establish their previous existence, their causal role, or the universality of the thesis.

Al-Ustādh Abū Isḥāq maintains that indivisible atoms are homogeneous and do not themselves vary in weight and lightness. Variation in the weight of bodies reflects **more atoms in the heavy body and fewer in the light one**. **Reply:** even conceding the homogeneity of atoms, a compound of few atoms might receive a property of heaviness and one with many a property of lightness by the voluntary Creator's will or other causes, just as compounds receive colours, flavours and other accidents.

A criticism of both views appeals to the **same waterskin filled first with water and then with mercury**. A given vessel holds mercury many times as heavy as the water it held, even though water is agreed to be more moist and the same volume is occupied. If the mercury's greater weight were simply due to a larger number of equal atoms, water must have been separated by large amounts of interstitial void proportional to that excess of weight. On that supposition one would expect to perceive far more empty regions than filled ones in the waterskin of water—leaving aside the prior concessions required that void exists and that the water does not naturally descend into those empty spaces, perhaps because of divine will or an alleged repulsive force of the void. One could reply that the interstices are not perceived because of their minuteness and their very close intermixture with the watery parts.

**On the words, “And the Qāḍī denied.”** Our theologians who affirm inclination disagree about its individuation. The Qāḍī holds that *iʿtimād* is **one accident in each body**, variously designated according to consideration: in relation to above it is called lightness, in relation to below heaviness, and it has no special established names for the other directions. When he is reported to allow multiple inclinations to coexist, his meaning is that one underlying thing admits various **considerations and relations** to the six directions. Others treat inclinations as **numerically multiple but not contrary** [the source's account of how these combine is incomplete at this point]. The argument then turns to counteracting felt pressures in differently directed attempts to move a weight.

title: Contrary inclinations; Muʿtazilite disputes about persistence and generated effects
en:
### Contrary inclinations; Muʿtazilite disputes about persistence and generated effects

When a heavy stone is drawn **upward**, a downward resistance is felt; if another attempts to pull it downward, an upward resistance may be felt. Similarly, when two people pull opposite ends of a rope with equal force, each experiences pressure in the rope against the direction of his pull. The correct position is that the two **natural inclinations**, absolute heaviness and lightness, are contrary and cannot coexist in one and the same thing in the same respect. But natural and **non-natural imposed inclination** need not be contrary. In a stone being lifted, the lifter experiences downward resistance from its nature while the upward mover supplies an imposed upward pressure.

As for two opposed **non-natural** inclinations, some hold them contrary—for example, one impulse rightward and another leftward—on the ground that inclination is the **proximate principle of motion**. If two such inclinations could coexist as fully efficacious principles, two opposed motions would occur intrinsically together, since a complete cause entails its effect. A body would then occupy two places in one instant. The word “intrinsically” is essential here: one body can have two differently directed movements when one is intrinsic and the other derivative, as with a passenger walking toward the stern of a ship which is moving toward the bow. This is the meaning of al-Jubbāʾī's claim that movements in contrary directions are opposed and hence the inclinations necessitating them are also opposed.

Al-Āmidī objects that this is a weak analogy without a shared ground: contrary effects need not entail different, much less contrary, causes. One nature can cause movement when outside its natural place and rest when it reaches its natural place. Besides, the impossibility of two opposite motions follows from their making a body occupy two places at once, whereas two impulses have no comparable immediate consequence. **Response to this line of proof:** if “proximate principle” means a **complete cause**, we deny that inclination alone is such a cause, since an impediment must also be absent. If it means a mere contributory principle, we deny that the effect must follow whenever it is present. Moreover, were the proof sound, natural and imposed inclinations would also be contrary by exactly the same argument.

Even if these premises are accepted, there is a counterexample: a rope pulled equally in opposite directions is experienced by both people as pressing against each pull. If the two inclinations were absolutely contrary, they could not coexist in it. One might reply that the rope merely resists movement like any other stationary body, without itself exercising two distinct impulses.

The Muʿtazilites call **natural inclination** *lāzim* (inherent or necessary), such as a heavy body's downward and a light body's upward tendency; **imposed inclination** is *mujtalab* (acquired or induced), such as forcing a heavy body up, forcing a light body down, or directing either sideways. They dispute several further questions.

**1. Does air have an inherent upward inclination?** Al-Jubbāʾī says it does. An inflated skin forcibly held underwater rises if released; if cut, its air escapes upward through the water. Even while attached to some heavy object, the skin may rise when the obstacle is removed. **Objection:** perhaps the air is merely pressed out by the surrounding water's weight. **Reply:** were air not naturally buoyant and directed upward through water, increasing the external pressure would cause it to settle more securely, as it does with other weights, not rise—particularly if the skin remains sealed.

Abū Hāshim denies that air has such an inherent tendency. If air naturally rose, the air lodged among the pieces of a wooden object floating in water would detach itself from the wood and ascend alone. Al-Jubbāʾī, he argues, has no other explanation of the wood's rising and floating than the separation of its parts and air's presence among them. **Objection:** the composite may acquire a condition binding its parts and preventing their separation; the air mixed into it may lose some of the force tending to separate, through tempering by mixture. **Reply:** our concern is with the portions of air **adjacent to the pieces of wood**, not air converted into a genuine constituent of the mixture, as philosophers describe some compounds. A better answer is that the entrapment of air among the wooden parts prevents it from separating and carries the surrounding material along when the air tends upward.

**2. Do inclinations persist?** Al-Jubbāʾī denies endurance to both inherent and imposed inclination. Abū Hāshim says that inherent inclination persists, as observation shows in colours and tastes. Al-Jubbāʾī argues, first, that a person pressing down upon a stone produces an imposed downward inclination which does not endure. Since it shares the most special character of the inherent inclination—being a downward inclination—the latter cannot endure either. Second, in other transient accidents such as sounds, there is no relevant difference between what an agent can produce and what he cannot. Likewise, since imposed inclinations are within power and inherent inclinations are not, their difference in power does not establish a difference of endurance. **Reply:** the most special characteristic may be **inherent** inclination rather than downwardness; and the comparison with sounds is analogy without a demonstrated common reason.

**3. Does inclination generate movement or rest?** Al-Jubbāʾī holds that it generates neither: **movement generates movement and rest**. Someone opening a door or throwing a stone must first move his hand before the lock or stone moves, and the lock's or stone's movement then generates its rest at the destination. Abū Hāshim holds instead that **inclination** generates both. If a vertical post is supported by a prop and someone pushes toward the prop, removing the prop makes the post move in that direction and fall, although the person pressing has not himself moved. Both arguments are weak: neither proves that only the proposed cause operates. In one case motion might generate the effect; in another, inclination might do so. The further suggestion that the stone's movement must precede the thrower's because the hand cannot enter the stone's location until the stone leaves it is likewise subject to qualifications, to be addressed next.

title: Philosophical *mayl*: natural, forced and psychic; transition to visible qualities
en:
### Philosophical *mayl*: natural, forced and psychic; transition to visible qualities

The earlier argument concerning the thrower's hand and stone ends thus. If the proposed priority is **temporal**, the exclusion of two bodies from one place does not entail it. The stone's leaving and the hand's entering can occur **together**, like the component parts of a rotating ring—indeed, so it must be if no separation is to intervene. If causal or essential priority is intended, the order goes the other way: the hand must move for the stone to move; thus one properly says, “The hand moved, and therefore the stone moved,” but not the reverse.

It is therefore more plausible that either **motion** or **inclination** may generate movement or rest. Inclination can produce different effects: some by itself and without an additional condition, such as generating movement in the sense previously described as its proximate principle; others by itself **with** a condition, as when it produces different spatial configurations through a body's movement, or returns a body to its natural place after the condition of its having left that place; and still others **indirectly**, as when it produces adjacency which generates combination, or the rupture of continuity which generates pain.

**On the words, “And the philosophers name it.”** The philosophers call inclination **mayl** and distinguish **natural**, **forced** and **psychic** (*nafsānī*) inclination. When its source and principle are **outside its subject**, it is forced, as in an arrow shot upward. Otherwise, if accompanied by intention and consciousness, it is psychic, as in a person pressing upon another thing. Otherwise it is natural, whether the relevant power acts continuously in the same way, as in a stone held in the air, or in different ways, as in a plant's tendency to spread and grow. Some call the consciously intended type **voluntary**, and make “psychic” broader than that, including the kind of natural inclination which does not proceed in one uniform manner and belongs to ensouled things; in that terminology a plant's inclination is also psychic. Others put such plant inclination outside the three classes on the ground that it is **composite**, as the discussion of movement will explain more fully.

The philosophers' further statements reveal uncertainty as to whether *mayl* means the **sensible pressure itself** or the **proximate source of pressure**, present when a stone ascends through air or rests upon the ground.

One claim is that natural inclination does **not** exist when a body has arrived at its natural place. Otherwise it must either incline toward that place, absurdly seeking what is already attained, or incline away from it, absurdly abandoning by nature what nature seeks. This argument does not apply to the **source** of inclination, whose effect can be absent through an unmet condition or an obstacle.

Another claim is that natural inclination cannot coexist with **forced inclination in the opposite direction**, since simultaneous active pressure **toward** and **away from** the same direction is plainly impossible. A stone shot upward consequently has no actually operating downward pressure, although it possesses the **potential** for one: it is constituted to exhibit that pressure when the imposed force's dominance ceases. Natural and forced inclinations *toward the same direction* can coexist. A stone driven forcibly downward has the downward pressure it would have by nature if left to itself, together with a further pressure produced by the external driver according to the driver's strength and intention. Its descent is therefore faster than a natural fall, and the degree of increase varies with the forcing agent's strength.

A third claim explains the motion of a stone thrown upward and later descending naturally. The imposed upward movement is strongest initially and weakens toward its termination; the natural descending movement becomes strongest in the opposite sequence. The **forced inclination** is progressively weakened by successive contacts and resistances of the air through which it passes, while the **natural inclination**—understood now as a source of pressure—gains in relative efficacy until the two are balanced. Thereafter the forced tendency continues to diminish and the natural one prevails, with descending movement increasing in speed.

A fourth argument for a natural principle of inclination points to two stones of unequal size thrown upward with the **same motive force**: their movements differ in speed even though the mover was the same. The allegedly relevant difference is that the larger stone bears **more opposing natural inclination** than the smaller. The Imām replies that **nature itself** is a power distributed through the body and divided according to the body's parts; more of this power exists in the larger body, giving it more resistance. Philosophers, however, describe nature as a stable thing which does not admit increase or decrease within one body, so that the nature of all the water and of some of it is the same. The issue cannot be resolved without a precise account of what is here meant by **nature**.

They offer several usages, none a complete real definition. Nature can mean what first produces movement and rest **intrinsically**, without awareness or will; what produces an effect which never fails to follow and requires no extrinsic cause, as with a stone's descent; what produces uniform movements without awareness; or, more broadly, any corporeal power. In medical writing “nature” may be used for **temperament**, a dominant quality among contrary qualities, innate heat, vegetal soul and similar notions; these uses concern composites particularly.

**On the words, “The second kind: the visible qualities.”** Philosophers hold that what is **primarily and intrinsically visible** consists of light and colour, although seeing colour presupposes light. Through these, other properties are seen **mediately**, including quantitative or positional determinations: magnitudes, orientations, straightness, curvature, convexity, concavity, other shapes, length, breadth, smallness, largeness, nearness, distance, separation, contact, motion, rest, laughter, weeping, beauty, ugliness and more. What seems to be direct vision of moisture, dryness, smoothness or roughness is really vision of their **concomitants**—flowing or cohesion, reducible to movement or rest, and the even or uneven disposition of parts in space.

title: Visible qualities: colours, species and gradational predication (*tashkīk*)
en:
### Visible qualities: colours, species and gradational predication (*tashkīk*)

**First investigation, on colours.** The real natures of colours—and indeed of all immediate sensibles—are evident and need no explanation. **Black and white** are clearly contraries because they stand at opposite extremities of colour. The intermediary colours, such as red and yellow, are distinct species with distinct effects according to careful investigators. They are not contraries if contrariety requires the **maximum difference** between opposites; they may be called contraries if that condition is dropped.

**On the words, “And the precise account.”** Philosophers ordinarily speak of the species of colour as blackness, whiteness, redness, yellowness and so on, and of tangible qualities as heat, cold, moisture, dryness and the like. But the more exact analysis is that genuine lowest species are **determinate grades** of whiteness whose individuals do not differ in intensity—for example, a particular whiteness of snow—and likewise for blackness and other colours, and for anything predicated by degrees (*bi-l-tashkīk*). A lowest species of tangible heat is not heat simply, but one determinate heat whose instances are equal, such as the heat of pure fire; a lowest species of visible brightness is not light in general, but a particular intensity whose instances agree, such as a determinate sunlight.

The confusion arises because several lowest species may share a property and a familiar name. Varieties of white are grouped together as **whiteness**, associated with the dilation or scattering of vision, and varieties of black as **blackness**, associated with contraction; likewise different grades of heat or cold. One then imagines each named group a single species. Different grades of light are not conventionally collected in the same manner under contrasting special names, so people do not always make the same grouping, but may instead imagine **all light** to be one lowest species. Colour and light belong to the same level among visible qualities, yet colour is a genuine genus of colour-species, whereas light, because it is predicated in different degrees, is not a genus of the grades under it in the account being reported. Light appears a single species because its different grades resemble one another; whiteness and blackness similarly appear individual species because their grades resemble one another. On this analysis “light” is like “whiteness”: neither a genus nor an ultimate species of its grades, but a **common accidental designation**.

The foundation is the philosophers' thesis that **predication by degrees can occur only in what is accidental**, since a quiddity and its essential constituents cannot vary in intensity. Consider whatever factor accounts for the higher degree and is present in the more intense case but absent from the weaker. If that factor lies *outside* the quiddity, the quiddity itself is the same in both and does not vary in degree. If it lies *inside*, the weaker case lacks an essential constituent and does not share that quiddity at all. Thus if the special determination belonging to **sunlight** but lacking in moonlight were part of the essence of light, moonlight would not be light; if it were not, their difference would not be a difference within the essence of light.

**Objection:** if that argument were sound, no *accidental predicate* could be graded either. The feature in the stronger subject either belongs to the definition of the common accident, in which case the weaker does not share the accident, or lies outside it, in which case the meaning of that accident is equal in both. For example, if the peculiarity of snow's whiteness, as compared with ivory's, entered the meaning of whiteness, ivory would not be white in that meaning; if it did not, whiteness itself would be equally present in both.

**Reply on behalf of the orthodox theory:** the additional feature belongs to the quiddity of the **more intensely qualified subject**, not to the quiddity of the common accident or of the weakly qualified subject. The fact that the additional determination is absent from the concept of the common accident does not mean that the accident must be manifested in every subject to exactly the same degree.

**Further objection:** the same move appears available for **quiddity itself**. If what is common to a range of subjects can vary in an accidental quality through a feature outside the common quality but within one subject's nature, why could a common essence not vary through a feature outside the common essence yet within one individual's own identity? Light might itself be the whole quiddity, or a genuine genus, of the varieties of light, with the special brightness of sunlight outside the common nature of light but part of the concrete identity of sunlight. The same reasoning applies in analogous cases.

More directly, we deny that a factor of increased degree which lies outside a shared essence necessarily leaves the shared essence **equal in every instance**. That would follow only if the addition were not **an addition of the same kind** as the thing qualified. Nor does it matter whether the extra degree enters the quiddity of the more intense subject or is one of its accidents. Suppose the extra intensity of sunlight were accidental to that light: the difference in brightness would still obtain. What matters is that it adds **light to light**, **whiteness to whiteness**, or **heat to heat**. The extra element in sunlight, snow-white and fire-heat is simply *more* light, white or heat. Why should an analogous additional degree be impossible in a quiddity and its essentials?

The upshot is a dilemma. If the fact that the additional feature is outside the shared meaning **prevents variation** within that meaning, then no shared predicate can vary among instances, whether accidental or essential—this is the counterexample. If it does not prevent variation, the philosophical argument against variation in essence has not been established.

For this reason some reject *tashkīk* altogether, accepting the reasoning universally. Others permit predication by degree even in quiddities and their essential constituents, because no demonstration rules it out. They appeal to the difference between longer and shorter **lines**: the extra length of the longer line is of the nature of line itself, and its line-nature seems more complete, even if the added length is not an essential constituent of “line” considered as such. A proposed distinction between additional factors that enter the more intense subject's quiddity and those that enter merely its individual identity must be justified. In any case the original argument would not establish that essential constituents cannot themselves be graded, for something by which a **genus** varies might lie outside the genus while entering the essence of some of its **species**.

title: Are colours real qualities or effects of transparency and reflection?
en:
### Are colours real qualities or effects of transparency and reflection?

**Second investigation.** Some maintain that **colour has no separate reality**. Whiteness is merely an appearance due to air intermingled with very small transparent particles, as in snow: the supposed cause is simply air penetrating the small transparent icy fragments and light entering them. The same is said of foam, powdered crystal and pulverized clear glass. Blackness is thought to appear when light cannot penetrate deeply into a body because it is dense and its parts closely packed. Other colours arise through differences of transparency and the degree to which air is mixed with the substance. Blackness is sometimes attributed to water insofar as it displaces air and prevents light reaching the underlying surface perfectly; thus a wet garment tends to look darker.

Careful investigators hold instead that colours are **genuine qualities**, not mere illusions. That the mentioned conditions produce some colours does not deny their genuine existence or their origination from **other causes**. Avicenna explicitly says that mixing air with a transparent medium is undoubtedly a cause of apparent whiteness, but whiteness can also arise differently. A boiled egg becomes whiter, although heat has not rarefied it and filled it with air; rather, it has driven the air out, as shown by the egg's increased heaviness. He also gives the example of a preparation called **“Virgin's Milk”** (*laban al-ʿadhrāʾ*): lead oxide or litharge is dissolved in heated vinegar and clarified until the vinegar is transparent; another solution is prepared in water that has been boiled with an alkaline material and thoroughly filtered. When the two clear liquids are mixed, the dissolved material coagulates into intense whiteness, after which it dries. This is not simply air entering separated transparent fragments, nor can it easily be reduced to reflection among particles brought close together, since the sharp alkaline solution might more naturally be expected to separate them. It is a **transformation of quality**. Likewise gypsum turns white under heating but does not become comparably white by fine grinding, although breaking its particles apart and admitting air would then be even more evident.

Thus Avicenna does not deny that snow, foam, powdered crystal and glass really appear white through admixture of transparent fragments and air. He maintains that **whiteness occurs by other causes too**, whereas previously he knew only this cause. Indeed, in one passage of *al-Shifāʾ* he says, “I do not know whether whiteness can arise from another cause.” The author of *al-Mawāqif* appears to have taken certain remarks of *al-Shifāʾ* about the appearance and visibility of a white colour in those familiar cases to mean that Avicenna denies real whiteness there, and consequently charged him with sophistry. The present discussion insists that this is a **misreading**, not Avicenna's position.

Two further arguments appear in *al-Shifāʾ* for the existence of whiteness independently of air mixed with transparent particles. **First**, there is not one route from white to black. One can pass from white through grayish tones and brown to black, from white through red and darkened red to black, or through green and dark blue to black. This diversity suggests different principles of colour composition. Were there only white and black, and were white merely the effect of air penetrating transparent matter, their combination should follow one ordered route, varying at most in degree. **Second**, red, green and other colours are **reflected**. If all colour differences were due merely to transparent bodies mixed with other material, only whiteness should be reflected from red and green, since independent blackness, according to experiment, is not reflected.

These arguments more clearly establish that different colours need not be produced merely by blending **black and white** than they establish that whiteness cannot arise through a mixture of air and transparent fragments. Even the purported entailments are doubtful: different modes of mixing black and white might produce different routes, and blackness mixed with other things might reflect even if blackness alone does not.

Some deny only the positive reality of **whiteness**, while accepting that blackness is real. They argue that whiteness departs and its subject receives other colours, whereas blackness does not behave so. Even if both claims are granted, a real quality might be **separable** and an appearance **persistent** because the cause of the former disappears while the condition producing the latter persists. **Objection:** a white subject can receive every colour, and whatever can receive something must be devoid of it, since being in potency to receive and already possessing are incompatible. **Reply:** the subject receives all colours **other than the white presently in it**; it need be devoid only of those. If “can receive” means sheer possibility compatible with present actuality, we deny that recipient and possession are incompatible. One might suggest that requiring every possible recipient to lack the property makes the recipient incapable of ever acquiring it. But the necessity is **conditional**, applying only *while* the subject remains in the relevant unactualized state.

**On the words, “And it was said.”** Among those who hold black and white to be genuine qualities, some make these **the two primary colours** and explain the others as mixtures. Mixing only white and black produces gray; mixing black with brightness, as in a sunlit cloud or smoke illuminated by fire, produces red when black predominates, deeper dark red when it strongly predominates, and yellow when brightness predominates. Yellow joined to illuminated black yields green; green with more black becomes leek-green, with white verdigris-green, and with black and a little red dark blue or indigo; this mixed with red produces purple, and so forth. Others distinguish **five** primary colours—black, white, red, yellow and green—and derive the rest through mixing. Observation shows that these combinations **can** produce the particular colours, but does not establish that such colours **can arise only through those combinations** and are not in themselves simple qualities. The completion of this objection follows in the next unit.

title: Light, illumination, shade and the theory that light consists of bodies
en:
### Light, illumination, shade and the theory that light consists of bodies

**Third investigation: light.** Like other primary sensibles, **light** (*ḍawʾ*) needs no real definition. Calling it “the quality which is the first perfection of the transparent qua transparent,” or “the quality through which things are seen without first seeing something else,” is to define what is evident through what is more obscure. These formulations are intended only to draw attention to particular properties.

If light belongs intrinsically to its bearer and is not received from facing another luminous body, it is **intrinsic light** (*dhātī*), as with the sun, termed **ḍiyāʾ**. Otherwise, as with the moon, it is **received or accidental light** (*ʿaraḍī*), termed **nūr**. This is related to the Qurʾānic description of the sun as *ḍiyāʾ*, possessing radiance of itself, and the moon as *nūr*, possessing received light. Received illumination which comes from directly facing an intrinsically luminous body—the moon's disc or the earth's sunward face—is called light **of the first degree**. That arising from facing something which is illuminated by another thing is second-, third-, and further-degree light: the earth's surface before sunrise may receive light from sunlit air; a room within a house may be illuminated by the air of the courtyard, itself illuminated through another region, and so on through intervening media. Eventually illumination ceases entirely; that is **darkness**, the absence of light in what is naturally suited to be illuminated.

Darkness is thus a **privation of light**, not an independent positive quality as some claim. Were it a positively existent quality obstructing vision, darkness surrounding someone seated in a cave would prevent him from seeing a person outside the cave in bright air, just as it prevents him seeing someone concealed in the cave itself. An intervening visual obstacle is not relevantly different merely because it surrounds the seer or the object. One could reply that darkness is no obstacle in itself: illumination of the **visible object** is simply a condition of being seen, absent inside the cave. But that answer is unavailable to those who explicitly maintain that darkness is a **positive quality which obstructs vision**.

Those who affirm darkness as positive appeal to the Qurʾānic statement that God “made the darknesses and the light,” since what is made must exist. The reply denies this premise. One can bring about **a determinate privation**, as in making someone blind. Only absolute undifferentiated nothingness is incompatible with production in the requisite sense.

**On the words, “And they are uncertain.”** Philosophical investigators agree that **air can be illuminated**. They dispute whether pure air itself bears the light or whether the light subsists in vapours, smoke particles, or other materials mixed with the air. Supporters of pure air's illumination appeal to the eastern sky's brightness before sunrise. They argue also that, were the air not luminous, stars situated in a direction opposite the sun would remain visible during the day, since nothing would prevent vision except the eye's being overpowered by stronger light. Both arguments are weak, since the issue is the status of **pure, unmixed air**. The Imām proposes that if brightness arose only from material admixture, purer air would necessarily be less luminous and more turbid, denser air more luminous—whereas experience seems to show the reverse. But this too is weak: admixture could help illumination up to a certain proportion and reduce it when excessive, as both deficiency and excess may be detrimental.

Those who deny light's inherence in pure air argue that, if light truly qualified the air, the air itself should appear illuminated like a wall, whereas air is invisible. **Reply:** visibility requires **colour** in addition to light; pure air has no colour.

**On the words, “As for shade.”** The term *ẓill* here concerns a certain degree of received illumination rather than sheer positive darkness: the light arising through an already illuminated medium, itself lit directly by sun or fire or indirectly by moonlight. Some define shade as received light or as a thing luminous only through another; but that would apply to the directly illuminated lunar body, which is not ordinarily counted as *shade*. The discussion in *al-Mawāqif* of endlessly varying grades of shade according to the size of an aperture—such as the amount of light admitted into a house through a large or small opening—rests upon the philosophical doctrine that bodies, magnitudes and their dependent quantities are endlessly divisible, even when contained within finite bounds. One cubit may allow indefinitely many possible divisions, at least in supposition. The principle that what is bounded on both sides must be **finite** concerns total continuous or discrete magnitude, not a limit to the possibility of division.

At times light seems to flicker, shine or undulate upon a body as though it were flowing out and wavering back and forth, almost concealing the body. If such effulgence is **intrinsic**, as with the sun, it is called a **ray** (*shuʿāʿ*); if received or reflected, as in a mirror, a **glint or brilliance** (*barīq*).

**Fourth investigation.** Some philosophers hold that light consists of **minute bodies** issuing from the luminous thing and reaching the illuminated object. Their argument is that light moves **in its own right**, and whatever is intrinsically moved is a body. The major premise is supposed evident: accidents move only in dependence upon the movements of their subjects. To support the minor premise, they point to the descent of sunshine from the sun to earth, the light following a lamp moved from place to place, and light's reflection from an encountered object to another. These, they say, are forms of movement.

**Reply:** we deny that light itself migrates. In every case **light originates afresh in the object facing the luminous source**. The appearance of transit is an illusion. The corpuscular view has further difficulties.

**First**, bodies moving by **nature** move upward or downward, not in every direction. Yet emitted light spreads in numerous directions, and its movement is neither externally forced nor a voluntary choice.

**Second**, if light were bodily, it could not traverse the immense interval from the solar sphere to earth in an instant, passing through the solid celestial spheres beneath it.

**Third**, a bodily light which is itself visible should **screen the body surrounded by it** from our view. The more intense its illumination, the more completely it would intervene between observer and object, whereas intense light ordinarily helps healthy vision. Even if it did not conceal its object entirely, the increased quantity of visible intervening matter should make the object harder, not easier, to see. In certain cases an intermediary can help someone with weak sight perceive fine lines by concentrating visual power, but that does not establish the general thesis. The corpuscular theorist may reply that these obstructive effects belong to **dense** bodies rather than transparent bodies, whereas the alleged corpuscles of light are transparent and their presence around an object is a **condition of seeing it**.

Those who deny light's inherence in pure air argue that, if light truly qualified the air, the air itself should appear illuminated like a wall, whereas air is invisible. Reply: visibility requires colour in addition to light; pure air has no colour.

On the words, “As for shade.” The term ẓill here concerns a certain degree of received illumination rather than sheer positive darkness: the light arising through an already illuminated medium, itself lit directly by sun or fire or indirectly by moonlight. One cubit may allow indefinitely many possible divisions, at least in supposition. The principle that what is bounded on both sides must be finite concerns total continuous or discrete magnitude, not a limit to the possibility of division.

At times light seems to flicker, shine or undulate upon a body as though it were flowing out and wavering back and forth, almost concealing the body. Their argument is that light moves in its own right, and whatever is intrinsically moved is a body. The major premise is supposed evident: accidents move only in dependence upon the movements of their subjects. To support the minor premise, they point to the descent of sunshine from the sun to earth, the light following a lamp moved from place to place, and light's reflection from an encountered object to another. These, they say, are forms of movement.

Reply: we deny that light itself migrates. In every case light originates afresh in the object facing the luminous source. The appearance of transit is an illusion. The corpuscular view has further difficulties.

First, bodies moving by nature move upward or downward, not in every direction. Yet emitted light spreads in numerous directions, and its movement is neither externally forced nor a voluntary choice.

Second, if light were bodily, it could not traverse the immense interval from the solar sphere to earth in an instant, passing through the solid celestial spheres beneath it.

Third, a bodily light which is itself visible should screen the body surrounded by it from our view. The more intense its illumination, the more completely it would intervene between observer and object, whereas intense light ordinarily helps healthy vision. Even if it did not conceal its object entirely, the increased quantity of visible intervening matter should make the object harder, not easier, to see. In certain cases an intermediary can help someone with weak sight perceive fine lines by concentrating visual power, but that does not establish the general thesis. The corpuscular theorist may reply that these obstructive effects belong to dense bodies rather than transparent bodies, whereas the alleged corpuscles of light are transparent and their presence around an object is a condition of seeing it.

title: Light's relation to colour; sound as a real sensible quality
en:
### Light's relation to colour; sound as a real sensible quality

**Fifth investigation on light.** The correct view is that light is a **quality distinct from colour**, not merely the **manifestation or disclosure of colour** as certain philosophers maintain. Light is a **condition of seeing colour**, not of colour's **existing**, as Avicenna maintains. Neither opposing view has a satisfactory proof, and each approaches denial of what is evident. Al-Rāzī's argument that a body's capacity to receive light depends on its already possessing colour, so colour could not depend on light without circularity, is weak. If “dependence” means **temporal or causal precedence**, its premise is disputed; if it means mere coexistence, no vicious circle follows. Al-Rāzī has himself acknowledged that light can exist without colour, as in the case of crystal visible at night.

**Third kind of sensible qualities: the audible, namely sounds and letters.** On our theological account, sound originates through **God's direct creation alone**, without air-waves, impact or separation having genuine efficient influence—just as every other originated thing is created. We often record the philosophers' false opinions without explicitly repeating their refutation, except where some further explanation is useful.

**According to the philosophers**, sound is a **quality arising in air** through a disturbance or wave (*tamawwuj*) caused by **impact** (*qarʿ*), violent contact, or **separation** (*qalʿ*), a violent tearing apart. This requires the struck or separated material to resist the striker or separator, as in striking water or tearing linen, unlike cotton whose resistance is insufficient. The “wave” is a condition analogous to waves on water, produced by successive impacts together with intervals of rest. Sound is not identical with the wave, impact or separation, as some suppose through confusing the quality with its **proximate or more remote cause**. The wave is not heard as such, though it can perhaps be felt by touch, while impact and separation can be seen.

Some imagine that sound **does not exist outside the perceiver**, but occurs in hearing only when the disturbed air reaches the ear's opening. Against this it is argued that, if sound existed solely in sensation, we could not hear **its direction** or distinguish a nearby from a distant sound, since by hypothesis the sound exists in no external place or direction. Yet when we hear a sound we know that it comes from right or left, near or far.

**Objection:** we could infer direction because the air-waves come from that direction, and infer distance because the impression of a nearby source is more powerful than that of a distant one, even if the sound itself is not in that direction or at that distance. **Reply to the first part:** if this were so, one could not recognize a source on the side opposite the ear actually used. A person may close his right ear, hear with his left a sound originating on the right, and recognize that direction, even though the disturbed air must bend around the head before reaching the left ear. **Reply to the second:** if strength alone indicated nearness, a strong distant sound would be confused with a weak nearby sound; two equally distant sources of different power would be judged to have different distances. This is not generally what occurs.

Another dispute is whether, when the disturbed air reaches the ear, what is heard is only the sound **in the air reaching the ear**, or also the sound existing in the **external air** through which it passed. The correct view on the philosophers' account is the latter, because the listener discerns a sound's original direction and distance. If sensing sound concerned only the air at the ear's opening rather than the external air at the beginning and middle of the path, the experience would be indistinguishable from a sound produced wholly within the ear: the source's direction and distance could not be recognized. Compare touch, which apprehends its object only when the object reaches the organ, not as located at the far end of a path; it cannot thereby discern whether the touched thing came from left or right, near or far.

Thus our recognition of direction and distance supposedly establishes two claims: **externally existing sound is itself apprehended**, and therefore **sound exists externally at that location**. In the Imām's formulation, since we distinguish the directions and distances of sounds, we must be perceiving external sounds **where they occur**, and we cannot apprehend them there unless they actually exist outside the ear.

**An objection:** hearing apprehends sound, not direction; the fact that sound is in a direction cannot itself be an audible object, or else hearing would be affected by different directions, whereas sound as sound does not differ with the location. **Reply:** saying that we hear the sound “in that direction” means that by hearing it we **know it to be there**; we do not thereby make direction itself a directly audible quality. Similarly, tasting sweetness or smelling fragrance from a body allows us to know that the quality belongs to that body, although the body as such is neither tasted nor smelled.

The proposed mechanism is that, once a sound is apprehended at the ear, the mind **follows it back attentively** through the wave which arrives and then through what preceded it, tracing the successive stages toward the source. If any portion of the wave persists to be traced, the subject discerns where it begins and ceases, its origin and direction, the distance of its source, and the decreasing strength of the disturbance. A distant sound is usually faint because the travelling disturbance weakens. Where no vestige survives by which the mind could retrace the route to the source, only the distance implied by the remaining vestige can be known.

**On the words, “And it indicates that perception of sound is by the arrival of air.”** Philosophers hold that when something produces a sound, the surrounding air becomes qualified by it, then successively adjacent air throughout the directions, to a range determined by the sound's strength. Only hearers within that range, to whose ears the affected air reaches, hear it.

They give several arguments. **First**, sound is carried or deflected by a blowing wind and may not be heard in the direction from which the wind blows, because the affected air fails to reach the listener's ear. Were air not carrying sound and hearing independent of its arrival, the pattern would be inexplicable. **Second**, when someone speaks loudly through a tube with one end in his mouth and the other at another person's ear, that person hears the voice while nearby bystanders may not. The tube, they argue, prevents the air bearing sound from reaching the others' ears. Further arguments follow.

title: Acoustic transmission, hearing through barriers and echo
en:
### Acoustic transmission, hearing through barriers and echo

**Third argument for the carriage of sound by air:** we see the visible cause of sound—an axe striking wood, for instance—before we hear the sound. The delay varies with the distance. If hearing did not depend on the **arrival of disturbed air**, this variation would be unexplained.

**Answer to all three arguments:** at most they show a constant concomitance; concomitance does not conclusively establish efficient causality. The way wind changes audible direction, the tube's restriction of sound to one listener, and the delay after the axe's strike could conceivably arise through other causes. These indications may yield **intuitive certainty** (*yaqīn ḥadsī*) to an observer, without constituting a demonstration compelling a disputant.

Those who deny dependence on the arrival of sound-bearing air offer counterarguments.

**First:** if only air at the ear were apprehended, we could not perceive the originating direction or distance. **Reply:** as already explained, on this theory the sound apprehended through the air's arrival is not restricted to the sound inhering in the air now touching the ear, as touch is restricted to immediate contact. It includes more distant sound, as occurs in sight.

**Second:** we hear the call of a muezzin although the wind carries the air away from our direction. **Reply:** some transmission remains possible even though the direct path is disrupted, which explains why hearing in such conditions is often disturbed.

**Third:** a solid wall may stand between listener and speaker. We can hear through it despite the apparent impossibility of the affected air passing through its pores while retaining its subtle waveform—an unstable disposition supposedly even more fleeting than writing traced upon water, a proverb for impermanence. **Reply:** if a barrier has absolutely no pores and there is no alternative route through which air could pass, we do not concede that a sound would be heard. Hearing grows weaker as the number and size of passages decrease. As to the waveform, if it means the actual **configuration of air** which prepares the production of sound, there is no need for that configuration to survive. It serves only as a **preparatory condition**. If “configuration” means the specific sound-quality or letter which results from it, there is no logical impossibility, indeed not a manifest improbability, in that quality persisting while the air passes through constricted openings.

Nevertheless, the hypothesis is extremely difficult to accept. Every portion of air throughout the affected region would need to bear a specific **nonabiding quality**, since everyone within that region hears it, and the extraordinarily subtle parts of air would need to preserve the same condition while moving in winds and forcing themselves through the pores of solid bodies.

An even greater difficulty concerns **echo** (*ṣadā*). The usual explanation is that an air-wave meets a smooth resisting body—a mountain or wall—which reflects the disturbance backward in its previous configuration, like a ball thrown against a hard wall. The reflected disturbance produces the echo. Philosophers differ whether it is the **same original wave** returning unchanged or a newly formed wave in the intervening air which acquires the returning wave's quality; the latter is more plausible. Either way, that the air should retain a nonpersistent quality after striking a solid barrier, return with its structure intact, generate the same quality in neighbouring air, and then lose it simply upon reaching the ear seems so improbable as almost to approach impossibility.

title: Letters, vowels, consonants and temporal structure of phonemes
en:
### Letters, vowels, consonants and temporal structure of phonemes

**Second investigation on the audible.** Sound can bear a quality through which it differs audibly from another sound **equivalent in pitch**, whether high or low. The quality is called a **letter** (*ḥarf*) in Avicenna's expression. Others call the **sound qualified by that quality** the letter; others, the **compound of the sound and its qualifying feature**. The last account seems nearest to the truth.

Equivalence in highness or lowness of tone is specified to exclude these tonal features from the intended distinguishing character: both can make sounds audibly different, but only when the tones already differ in pitch. “Differ **in what is heard**” excludes length, shortness, fragrance and other distinctions that do not distinguish the audible object as audible, though whether these are themselves qualities raises difficulties. Perhaps the better contrast concerns features like **nasalization** and **hoarseness**. A question remains whether “difference in what is heard” means that the **differentiating feature must itself be audible**, and whether pitch is directly audible while nasalization and hoarseness are not. The correct interpretation is that a difference *in the audible* means a difference **in the audible sound itself** such that sound is different when the determining feature differs and the same when it is the same. This holds of letters. Nasalization, hoarseness and similar conditions can vary while the phonemic identity of the sound remains the same, and vice versa.

What is said in *al-Ṭawāliʿ*—that letters are qualities qualifying sounds, by which sounds differ “in heaviness and lightness”—has no straightforward meaning. Perhaps its author understood “in heaviness” as qualifying an omitted phrase “from another sound equal to it in heaviness,” intended lightness to mean high pitch, and omitted the familiar requirement of difference in what is heard. Such an account is seriously confused. The truth is that defining letters in this fashion explains what is already clear by something less evident; its purpose is presumably merely to detail certain properties of a familiar sensible.

**On the words, “It is divided into silent and voiced.”** The three short vowels or *ḥarakāt* are counted among letters and called the **short sounded elements** (*muṣawwitāt maqṣūra*). The letters **alif, wāw and yāʾ**, when quiescent and developed from corresponding vowels—alif from *fatḥa*, wāw from *ḍamma*, yāʾ from *kasra*—are called the **prolonged sounded elements** (*muṣawwitāt mamdūda*). In Arabic these are the **letters of prolongation** (*ḥurūf al-madd*), because they are, as it were, extensions of the short vowels. Everything other than the sounded elements is called **silent** (*ṣāmit*), including wāw and yāʾ when bearing a vowel and when quiescent but not preceded by their corresponding vowel. Alif is always sounded: the use of the name “alif” for the glottal stop (*hamza*) is an equivocation of names.

The “movement” and “rest” (*ḥaraka*, *sukūn*) under discussion are **not** the local motion and rest characteristic of bodies. A vowel is rather a phonetic modification of a consonant through an inclination of its articulation toward the articulation of one of the prolonged vowels: toward alif is **fatḥa**, toward wāw **ḍamma**, and toward yāʾ **kasra**.

No one disputes the inability to begin a word with a **prolonged vowel** in the relevant form. The dispute is whether this is due simply to its quiescence, so that beginning with any silent unvowelled consonant is also impossible, or due to its **nature as an extended element deriving from full prolongation of a preceding corresponding vowel**, which can occur only after a consonant already bearing that vowel. The latter is correct. Anyone with intact pronunciation can recognize the possibility of beginning with a quiescent consonant in principle, although Arabic linguistic usage rejects this, just as it normally rejects pausing on a vowelled letter or combining two quiescent consonants except at a pause (for example, *Zayd* and *ʿAmr*). Where the first consonant is a **soft letter** and the second assimilated, combinations also occur, as in the cited examples, just as when the first is a prolonged vowel (e.g. *dābba*). Some speakers' inability to begin with a quiescent letter does not establish intrinsic impossibility; weakness of the organ can likewise prevent the pronunciation of perfectly possible sounds.

A proof from the claim that a prolonged vowel always requires a consonant, while a consonant could not require a subsequent vowel without circularity, is also unsuccessful. The prolonged vowel requires a **preceding consonant**, while the word-initial consonant would require a **following short vowel**; these requirements can be realized together without an impossible causal circle.

**Another division** distinguishes **instantaneous** (*ānī*) and **temporally extended** (*zamānī*) letters. A letter that can be prolonged, such as *fāʾ*, is extended. One that cannot be held, such as *ṭāʾ*, is instantaneous. The latter occurs at the beginning of releasing the breath, as in the cited example *ṭalaʿa*, or at the final instant of arresting it, as in *ghalaẓa*. A consonant occurring in the middle of a word, as in *baṭala*, may be treated in either way. An instantaneous phoneme qualifies sound as a **boundary** qualifies an extension, like point in relation to line. Some instantaneous letters resemble extended ones, such as *ḥāʾ* and *khāʾ*: their individual articulation supposedly cannot be indefinitely extended, but numerous similar utterance-elements occur in rapid succession without the senses distinguishing their separate moments, so they are experienced as one letter.

**On the words, “And into similar...”** The further classification treats the 29 traditional letters of Arabic, and phonemes in other languages, as distinct kinds, while allowing individuating differences among occurrences of a single kind. This continues in the next segment.

### Phonemic identity, syllables, speech, tastes and smells

The 29 consonantal and vocalic letters recognized in Arabic, together with sounds peculiar to other languages, are **distinct phonemic kinds** (*anwāʿ*), whereas instances of one sound may differ in individuating accidents. For example, the unvowelled **yāʾ** pronounced by Zayd now, by him later, or by ʿAmr differs in individual realization; without reference to the speaker, instances of a phoneme can agree in having **sukūn**, or *fatḥa*, *ḍamma* or *kasra*, or can differ in these features. This is the intended distinction between **likeness and difference through an accident**. An objection based on technical terminology—if “likeness” means same essence, different accidents cannot oppose it; if it means same accidents too, no two occurrences are alike, since numerical plurality requires some distinction—is answered by distinguishing identity of essential kind from agreement in a relevant accidental feature.

**On the words, “And the consonant with a vowel.”** Some later writers misunderstood the familiar classification of **syllables** (*maqāṭiʿ*). Al-Fārābī, Avicenna, the Imām and others explain that a consonant joined to a **short vowel** is a *short syllable*, such as *la*, *lu* or *li*. A consonant joined to a **prolonged vowel** is a *long syllable*, such as *lā*, *lū*, *lī*. A short syllable followed by an unvowelled consonant, such as *hal*, *qul*, *baʿ*, can also be called a long syllable because it occupies the **same metrical weight**.

**Objection:** why complicate the account? A long syllable is merely a consonant with a short vowel plus a following quiescent element, whether that element is a vowel of prolongation, as in *lā*, or a consonant, as in *hal*. Thus a syllable is simply a consonant with a vowel, or a vowelled consonant followed by a quiescent element; the former is short, the latter long. **Answer:** the latter type, *hal*, involves two consonants and an intervening short vowel, whereas *lā* consists fundamentally of **a consonant and a prolonged vowel**, not a further short vowel separately inserted between them, contrary to some grammatical descriptions. A prolonged vowel is the **full extension of the corresponding short vowel**, which is included within it as part of the extended sound. Hence short vowels are called **parts of letters of prolongation**.
**On the words, “And speech is composed of letters.”** Speech (*kalām*) is described as an ordered combination of **audible, distinguishable letters**. “Audible” excludes written or merely imagined letters; “distinguishable” excludes undifferentiated calls of birds. Speech divides into meaningless utterances and conventionally assigned expressions. Assigned expressions divide into **simple** and **compound**; simple expressions into **noun, verb and particle**; compound expressions into **complete**, permitting a meaningful pause, and incomplete.

Sometimes *kalām* is reserved for **meaningful expression**, that is, an utterance signifying a relation on which one can appropriately stop, whether **performative**—“Stand!”, “Is Zayd standing?”, “Perhaps Zayd is standing”—or **assertoric**, like “Zayd is standing.” Such speech may be a single short syllable, such as the imperative *qi*, a single long syllable such as *qī* or *qū*, or a combination of syllables. Sometimes *lafẓ* is instead reserved for what is composed of syllables and contrasted with a single letter or syllable. Thus one may say that the constituents of a composite expression are **words**, **letters** or **syllables**. *Zayd qāʾim* has two words; an expression like *yā-dā* may be analyzed into two syllables; *yā Zayd* into a syllable and a word; the feminine imperative *raʾī* into a syllable and a letter; and forms such as *arḍī* and *ikhshaw* into a word and a letter. One may object that *qī* and *qū* are each only one prolonged syllable. The reply may distinguish two letters—the consonant and the long vowel. A single short imperative such as *qi*, on the other hand, can be described as a short syllable together with the implicit pronoun **“you”**. In *qī* and *qū* the yāʾ and wāw serve as explicit grammatical indicators, so the same analysis does not posit a second hidden pronoun.

**On the words, “And al-Fārābī claimed.”** He classifies speech under **quantity**, and subdivides discrete quantity into the abiding, namely **number**, and the nonabiding, namely **spoken expression**. His argument is that speech has parts by which it is measured, and whatever is measured by its own parts is quantity. Syllables, short and long, are constituents of words and may be arranged into greater and greater structures: a short and long syllable in succession, or the reverse, followed by further combinations. The smallest measures are simple short syllables, then long syllables, then compound syllabic structures. Some expressions are measured by one such unit and others by two or more, just as some spatial magnitudes can be measured by one cubit and others by several. **Reply:** we deny that everything measurable by parts is intrinsically quantity. Such measurability must belong to the thing **of itself**. Speech is quantified only through **the number of its constituent units**, just as a body is measured by a cubit through the continuous quantity inhering in it.

**Fourth kind of sensible quality: tastes.** A familiar account makes the **nine primary tastes** arise from three states of the acting principle—heat, cold and an intermediate condition—combined with three states of the recipient—subtle, dense and intermediate. The existence of those effects and their causal explanations are discussed in more extensive works. These nine elementary tastes combine into indefinitely numerous mixed tastes, varying through combinations, degrees of strength and weakness, and tactile qualities mingled with them so closely that sense does not easily separate the constituents. Some compounds bear special names: **bushāʿa**, a mixture of bitter and astringent qualities in a certain medicinal extract, and **zuʿūqa**, a mixture of bitter and salty qualities found in a named plant. Other combinations have no distinct names, such as sweet and pungent notes in cooked honey, bitter and bland in chicory, or bitter, pungent and astringent in eggplant.

The **astringent** (*qābiḍ*) contracts the tongue's surface; the **harshly astringent** (*ʿafiṣ*) contracts both its surface and interior. “Blandness” (*tafāha*) as a taste means the character found in meat and bread. The term is also used for something with no taste whatever, such as the simple elements, or what cannot be tasted because no portion dissolves into the moist saliva except through special treatment, as with iron. The claim that only this last sense counts among tastes is contradicted by the account of chicory's mixed taste as **bitter and bland**, not purely bitter.

**Fifth kind: smells.** No special investigation is required here. The author then turns from the sensed qualities to further questions about their conditions and the qualities of living beings.

title: Psychological qualities: life, its prerequisites and its powers (I.221–222)

### Psychological qualities: life, its prerequisites and its powers (I.221–222)

The expressions *visible things*, *audible things*, *tangible things*, *tastes* and *smells* correspond to the five kinds of sensible quality, and can serve almost as their names. Linguistic usage is not uniform: a term sometimes denotes the quality, sometimes its subject, and sometimes both; likewise, the verbal noun may name the perception itself, as do seeing and hearing, or the action leading to it, as in the remaining senses. Thus one says “I saw the rose and its redness,” “I heard the sound,” but not “the sounding thing”; “I touched silk,” not “its softness”; “I tasted the food and its sweetness,” and “I smelt amber and its fragrance.”

**“The second division [of quality].”** These are the qualities peculiar to beings possessing animal souls. This means that among bodies they belong to animals, not plants or inanimate things. It does not preclude some such qualities in immaterial beings, including, according to some doctrines, God; but those who affirm divine life, knowledge and power do not thereby classify divine attributes as qualities or accidents. A psychological quality, when entrenched or established, is termed a **habit/disposition** (*malaka*); otherwise a **state** (*ḥāl*). The distinction may be accidental to an underlying condition: a state can become a habit. Nevertheless, to say that the numerically same individual or accident remains under wholly altered individuating circumstances is, strictly speaking, not without difficulty: the child and the old person are called the same person, although their individualizing accidents have changed.

**“Among them is life.”** Divine life will be considered separately. Definitions of corporeal life vary not primarily because philosophers disagree over its reality but because it is difficult to apprehend and express apart from concomitants and effects. It has been defined as a quality entailing sensation and movement conditional upon a balanced temperament; or as the power from which powers of sensation and movement originate; or as a power attendant upon the temperament appropriate to the species, from which animal perceptive and locomotive faculties emanate. The last description should be understood in terms of the **specific, varietal, and individual equilibrium** of temperament. Every natural species has an optimum complexion, departure from which destroys its specific organization; each variety and each individual also possesses a fitting equilibrium. When an organism acquires the equilibrium suitable to its animal kind, the power of life is bestowed and, by God's permission, external and internal senses and movements seeking advantage and avoiding harm proceed from it. Thus life presupposes equilibrium on this account, and is the source, not simply the aggregate, of perception and movement. It differs from nutrition, which also occurs in plants.

This argument requires proof that life really is a principle **distinct from** the faculties of sensation and motion, and that nutrition in plant and animal is the same kind of capacity. As evidence, thinkers point to a paralysed animal limb, which remains alive without feeling or voluntary motion, and a withered limb, which remains alive without being nourished. Al-Rāzī objects: failure of an operation does not prove absence of its power. The power may remain while an obstacle prevents its exercise. The reply is that the power actually producing characteristic vital effects—for instance, preserving a limb from putrefaction—remains when the powers actually producing sensation, motion, or nutrition do not operate. This is the sense suggested by the *Talkhīṣ al-Muḥaṣṣal*; it does **not** license redefining a power as something that invariably acts at present. Indeed a paralysed limb may retain sensitive and moving powers while being prevented from acting. The reply itself permits a further challenge: why not suppose **one** life-power responsible for every effect, hindered in certain manifestations by particular obstructions? The distinction between life and such specifically visual, auditory, other animal, and vegetative powers nevertheless remains clear.

**“According to us it is not a condition.”** Most mutakallimūn deny that life, simply as an attribute, intrinsically requires bodily constitution (*binya*), balanced temperament (*mizāj*), or animal spirit (*rūḥ ḥayawānī*). God could create it in a simple body, indeed in an indivisible atom. Constitution here means the body composed of the four elements; animal spirit is conceived as a subtle vaporous body generated from the finer humours, passing from the left cavity of the heart through arteries. Philosophers and many Muʿtazilites, relying on observed loss of life when the organism is dissolved, temperament unbalanced, or circulation blocked, affirm the dependence. But observed concomitance does not establish **necessary** dependence. One attempted proof of the contrary argues that, if life necessarily depended on constitution, either a single accident of life would inhabit several atoms, contrary to the rule that an accident has only one subject, or each atom would have its own life. In the latter case, mutual dependence creates a circle, and independent establishment in all similar atoms seems to lack a differentiating reason. If only some atoms received life, those alone, not the composite, would be living. These deductions remain controversial; their replies follow.

title: Death; perception as the presence of a thing or its form (I.223–224)
en:
### Death; perception as the presence of a thing or its form (I.223–224)

The preceding argument against life depending upon composition has several answers. A **single** attribute can belong to the composite as a **whole**, not thereby subsist in two subjects in the prohibited sense. Or each part can have life, with its possession of life depending on the others by **concomitance** rather than precedence, eliminating the vicious circle. Or the life of one part may depend on life in another part because of an external differentiating circumstance not known to us. The suggestion that the latter makes life independent of composition is invalid: not depending on **another part's life** does not entail not depending on **the existence of that other part** constituting the composite.

**“As for death.”** Death is the disappearance of life, i.e. the absence of an attribute from a subject that actually had it. This is a **privation** of life, like blindness supervening after sight, not every conceivable absence of life; thus a fetus merely ready to receive life is not automatically dead. On this account death is not positive. Others take it to be a **positive quality contrary to life**. This interpretation can explain the Muʿtazilite statement that death is an act of God or an angel bringing bodily life to an end without injury, the last qualification distinguishing it from killing. But if *act* means the causal action, not its effect, it defines **causing death**, not death itself. The verse concerning God's creating death and life does not conclusively make death a positive entity: *creation* there may mean determining or ordaining, embracing privation as well as existence, or the expression may suppress an understood genitive—creating **the causes** of death. Although such readings depart from the immediately apparent sense, they suffice to defeat a purported necessary proof.

**“Among them is apprehension/perception (*idrāk*).”** The investigators among the philosophers finally describe apprehending a thing as the **presence** (*ḥuḍūr*) of the thing before the intellect, either by its **own reality** or by a form abstracted from the thing or first produced in the intellect; the form is impressed either in the apprehender or in the organ by which apprehension occurs. This is the meaning of Avicenna's description in the *Ishārāt*: a thing's reality is represented before the apprehender and witnessed by that through which it apprehends. “Representation” includes presentation of reality itself or an image; the image can be derived from an external thing or arise directly, and inhere in the subject or organ. “Witnessing” means presence, **not** necessarily eyesight or direct sight of the external individual. The reference to the means of apprehension differentiates cognition without an organ, where the form is in the intellect itself, from cognition through an organ. Visual apprehension, according to one physiological theory, depends on an image in the crystalline humour; common-sense apprehension may concern an imaginative form in a neighbouring seat.

The expression can be criticized for verbal repetition in intellectual cognition, because the knower and its cognitive instrument are the same; and for implying two presences in sensory cognition, at the soul and at its organ. The intended meaning is not two independent presences: the presence at the sense belongs to perception by the soul.

When we cognize something, a **new state** manifestly arises in us. Natural awareness suggests the coming-to-be of a positive representation, not just the removal of something earlier. This is the thing's becoming manifest and distinguishable before the intellect. It cannot consist simply in the thing's external existence: nonexistents and impossibilities can be conceived, and external things can exist while escaping our understanding. The cognitive presence consists rather in an effect appropriate to the thing, such that if it were externally instantiated it would correspond to that thing. This is what philosophers mean by obtaining the form, the form's presence and impression, the soul reaching its object, and the like. The objection that *apprehension* is an attribute of the apprehender whereas *presence* is an attribute of a form does not refute the intended account; nor does the circularity objection from naming the apprehender in the definition, since it denotes the thing conventionally called an apprehender without using its disputed essential account. One may take the statement as an exposition of an initially evident meaning rather than a strict definition.

**“Either by its own reality.”** The apprehended object either is not outside the subject (as in self-apprehension and certain attributes of the soul), or is external and material, or is external and immaterial. In self-apprehension the reality present is allegedly the very subject already present, making cognition constant; material external things are apprehended through an abstracted form; immaterial separable things through a form not needing to be abstracted from material external reality. There are objections to the first thesis. It implies continuous knowledge of all one's states, although their existence and essence may require careful investigation. It seems to require two distinct terms for the relation of presence, making self-knowledge impossible. Finally, if the subject knows itself and its cognition and the cognition of that cognition, actual infinitely many cognitive acts follow. The philosophical reply appeals to distinctions **in consideration**: one immaterial reality can be regarded as seeing, seen, and sight, without positing infinitely many independent beings. Yet the claim of constant self-awareness requires an answer to the original experiential objection.
