### Mental representation: identity, inherence, and epistemic presence (I.225–226)

The account of self-knowledge by distinction in consideration comes to the claim that the single immaterial apprehender is not absent from itself. Considered as the one witnessing it is the knower, as witnessed the known, and as witnessing the knowledge. Its existence and presence are not numerically additional external facts. But al-Rāzī and other critics raise substantial difficulties about the alleged **form of the known thing**.

**First objection.** If a cognitive form were the very quiddity of what is represented, imagining heat or roundness would make the intellect hot or round, and conceiving heat and cold together would make it subject to contraries. **Reply:** having an **external individual realization** of heat as a quality inhering in one is not having its abstract intelligible nature as an object. The individual is invested with particularizing accidents and causes effects in the world; the universal form, abstract from those, does not impart the thing's natural operation. Equality of content means the intelligible, *if externally realised*, would be that quiddity; it does not mean that the external hot thing has entered the intellect. Thus one can call a mental form equal to the quiddity of the heavens or the same quiddity **under an intellectual consideration** without confusing modes of existence.

**Another reply** distinguishes the many senses of **“obtaining” (*ḥuṣūl*)**: property belonging to an owner, colour inhering in body, velocity ascribed to motion, form informing matter, or a present thing being before a witness—and the corresponding converse ascriptions. From one accident inhering in its subject follows **qualification by that accident**, but from something being cognitively present does not follow that qualification. The particular kind of presence is familiar in experience, although one may not define it except as cognition, awareness or encompassing a quiddity. Knowing fidelity, infidelity, generosity or avarice does not make one faithful, unbelieving, generous or miserly. Still less does knowing heat or circularity make the soul actually heated or circular. Conversely it remains disputed whether an accident's **informational or qualifying inherence** in a sentient subject entails the subject's knowledge of it. Nor can one infer, from a warm stone's having heat, that it cognizes heat. Simply calling all possession “presence” confuses these relations.

**Second objection.** It is the **external thing itself**—this blackness, sound, human being—that we know, not an image instead; replacing its object with a phantom appears to be sophistry. **Reply:** the external existent is indeed **the object**; its cognition occurs *by the presence* of a corresponding form. The medium of knowing is not being substituted for what is known.

**Third objection.** If the sense organ contains the form, then on the identification of perception with the form's occurrence the organ, not the soul or common sense, would be the perceiver. **Reply:** perception is the form's being present **to the perceiver** through its occurrence at the organ; the physical seat of the occurrence is not by itself the personal apprehender. Hence mere presentation at a sense without the soul's attention does not amount to a conscious act of cognition.

**Fourth objection.** The scientific form, as an accident of a particular soul, cannot match an external **substance**, let alone be the substance's quiddity. Being an individual accident, how can it be a **universal**? Moreover, philosophers sometimes call knowledge the form and sometimes its *obtaining*, although these are different notions. **Reply:** the contradiction only arises if one thing under **one and the same consideration** is at once substance and accident, individual and universal. An intelligible representation is an accident **as currently present in a subject**, but it represents a substance in that its intelligible content, *if it were externally realised*, would exist without a subject. Similarly, the mental event is particular as occurring in one soul, but universal in the scope of things to which its abstract content can correspond. It would be impossible only for one externally realised quiddity under one respect to be both inhering and noninhering.

As the distinction between a quiddity and its existence is conceptual, so the distinction between mental content and its *occurrence in the intellect* need not imply **two independent things**, a receptive mental form and then a second existent accident called presence. In this respect philosophers use “knowledge” both for the form and for its occurrence. But an important difficulty survives: knowledge surely appears to be an **externally actual mental quality**, existing in the soul through genuine inherence, whereas the form considered merely as a represented quiddity has not that kind of existence. This objection should not be dismissed; the following investigation confronts it directly.

title: Two considerations of a mental form; theologians' relational account of knowledge (I.227–228)
en:
### Two considerations of a mental form; theologians' relational account of knowledge (I.227–228)

The objection that a cognitive state is a genuinely **inhering accident** of the soul whereas a represented quiddity merely has an intentional or non-rooted mode of existence is powerful—indeed, al-Taftāzānī says that most difficulties directed against defining cognition as the obtaining of a form have this character. A tentative reply is to distinguish two considerations of the form. Considered in its **mental actual occurrence**, it is an external-quality-like accident genuinely inhering in and qualifying the soul. Considered solely according to its **intelligible quiddity** and without that occurrence, it is the representation of an object that may in the world be a substance, and does not itself qualify the soul in the way the external quality would. In the second consideration it has only non-independent intellectual existence. Calling the form itself “the known” is then a transferred usage, for properly the known is the thing whose form it is. The form may itself, however, become the subject of a second act of intellection and acquire properties not corresponding to anything external—those are **second intelligibles** (*maʿqūlāt thāniya*). Under this description universality is ascribed to **the mental intelligible**, while the externally existing individual is called universal only in the derivative sense that its abstract mental form is universal.

He quotes the *Mawāqif* as reporting that, for philosophers, what is present in the intellect is both knowledge and the known; an “intelligible human being is universal” means either that the form abstracted from individualization is universal or that what is known through it is universal. A critical distinction is necessary: if “the known” merely names the mental form, these two alternatives do not differ, nor does the phrase “through it” accomplish anything. If it names the external object, that is externally particular, not universal.

**“And the mutakallimūn.”** Those who deny mental existence and the obtaining of a form often characterize knowledge as **a bare relation and attachment** (*iḍāfa wa-taʿalluq*) between knower and known, or as a quality carrying that relation. On the second theory the quality is **knowledge** and the relation is the knower's being-knowing (*ʿālimiyya*). Al-Qāḍī further distinguishes one or even two additional relations beyond knowledge and being-knowing, yielding three or four entities for analysis. Other forms of perception are treated analogously. The difficulty of self-knowledge—relation ostensibly demands two terms—may be answered by diversity in consideration, as above.

A more serious problem concerns **knowledge of nonexistents**, including possible geometric configurations never actually realized, and **impossibilities** posited in proofs by contradiction. If they exist neither in the external world nor in an intellect, there are no terms for the relation of knowledge. Appealing to independently existing Platonic exemplars or inaccessible external bodies cannot give impossible objects an independent existence. One might respond that this establishes mental representation only for nonexistents; but **apprehension has a common meaning** across cases, varied by subjects and objects, and one cannot arbitrarily identify it with a bare relation in all other cases.

The defender of the relational theory can retort: even on the image theory there is no **external bearer** of the image of an impossible thing, and if some other known thing must accompany the image **in the mind**, there would be two mental things where only one has been allowed. The answer is that one **intelligible form alone** is present. Saying it is a form *of* the impossible means that were its object able to be realised externally, its corresponding intelligible content would be as that object; this does not assert the impossible actually exists. The form, in its mental occurrence, is the knowledge qualifying the soul; in its abstract intelligible nature it is the known under a nonindependent mode of existence. External objects differ: their corresponding things exist outside, while the knowledge is in the mind. This also qualifies the rule that a scientific form must correspond to something outside: for merely possible or impossible objects, correspondence is hypothetical and intelligible, not a relation to an actual external counterpart.

An important qualification appears in **Avicenna's *Shifāʾ***: he apparently concedes that an absolute impossibility such as the coincidence of contradictories cannot be given a genuinely positive unified image in the intellect. We conceive it by analogy—knowing a relation of conjunction between black and sweet and judging that a comparable conjunction cannot hold between black and white—or by judgment of **negation**: no such conjunction is possible. Thus the *Mawāqif* interprets Abū Hāshim's statement that knowledge of the impossible is knowledge **without a known thing**, for a “thing” in his terminology excludes the impossible. Al-Rāzī's charge of contradiction assumes a wider definition of “known”; there is no need to resolve it by the purely stipulative definition attributed to al-Āmidī. This is a critical boundary of the representation account, not a simple affirmation of independently existing impossible objects.

title: Species of perception and degrees of certainty (I.229–230)
en:
### Species of perception and degrees of certainty (I.229–230)

**“Second investigation.”** The philosophers distinguish four kinds of cognition by the materiality and individuation of what is apprehended. **Sensation** (*iḥsās*) perceives an object existing in **matter presently before the apprehender**, under its particular surrounding characteristics, such as shape and position. **Imagination** (*takhayyul*) apprehends the particular object with these sensible characteristics even when the object is absent. **Estimation** (*tawahhum*) apprehends nonsensible intentions such as certain qualities or relations belonging to this **material particular**. **Intellection** (*taʿaqqul*) apprehends the thing according to what it is in itself, not according to the extraneous individuating conditions, either in isolation or together with other intelligibly apprehended attributes. Sensation requires three conditions—presence of the material thing, sensory circumstances, and particularity; imagination dispenses with the first; estimation with the first two; and intellection with all three. The intelligible form remains an individual occurrence in a particular soul, but this is a **mental** circumstance, not the material conditions abstracted from. The classification of those latter characteristics as genuinely mental accidents has already been disputed in the section on quiddity.

**“According to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, sensing a thing is knowing it.”** Sight is knowledge of visibles, hearing of audibles, and likewise the other senses. Most theologians object that there is a manifest difference between **knowing all about this colour** and actually **seeing** it, between knowing a sound and hearing it, and between knowing a smell and smelling it. A defender can deny another way of knowing exactly the sensed particular, or concede two species of knowledge differing essentially or individually. The first denial is implausible: one can make judgments concerning a colour after it disappears. The second yields the critics' point: sensory cognition is not numerically the same species as another knowledge arising by inference, inspiration, or intuitive apprehension. The issue then becomes partly terminological: does “knowledge” name every apprehension or a distinct kind? Ordinary language does not naturally call bare sensing *knowledge*.

Technical use varies. Knowledge may be reserved for **universals**, or for **composite apprehension**, distinguishing acquaintance (*maʿrifa*) as apprehension of particulars or simples. It may also mean only **certainty** (*yaqīn*) among judgments, comprising **firm assent, correspondence to reality, and stability**. Lacking firmness is *ẓann* (opinion); lacking truth is **compound ignorance**; lacking stability is the imitative belief of a follower. Or belief may include both true and false convictions; or “knowledge” may broadly signify every judgment; and “opinion” may mean all convictions short of certainty.

Some say certainty includes an additional judgment that the contradictory is impossible, while mere opinion includes a judgment that the contradictory is possible, though less probable. The more exact account does not require two explicit judgments: a certain belief is one such that, **if the contradictory were considered**, the believer would pronounce it impossible; opinion is such that the believer would allow its possibility. Thus each is a **single** judgment.

The required **stability** cannot mean mere psychological obstinacy, since a follower can believe tenaciously. If it means impossible loss of conviction, even demonstrated conclusions may be doubted when their premises are forgotten. We answer: mere lack of the conclusion's present explicit consideration need not introduce doubt; but if the epistemic premises have vanished such that a fresh demonstration must be acquired, the belief is **no longer certain at that moment**. Certainty excludes doubt **while it remains certainty**.

The classes of genuine judgment are then knowledge, compound ignorance, correct imitative belief, and opinion, since an unfirm judgment must favour one side. Some later writers distinguish opinion, **doubt**, and **conjectural apprehension of the disfavoured side** (*wahm*) as three degrees of unfirm judgment. Al-Taftāzānī objects: *shakk* is indecision between affirming and denying, while *wahm* is considering the weaker alternative; neither is itself judgment or assent. If “doubt” means assenting to the proposition that two possibilities appear equal, that is simply **a judgment about one's own indecision**, not assent to either side of the original question.

**“Distraction/forgetfulness.”** *Sahw* and *nisyān* are sometimes distinguished, sometimes used synonymously. Relative to knowledge they are a **privation after possession**, like death relative to life. Doubt is privation of assent and thus simple ignorance at the level of judgment, although it may involve correct apprehension of its terms. **Compound ignorance** is a firm false belief, “compound” because one is ignorant of the facts **and ignorant of one's ignorance**. It is opposed to knowledge as a contrary positive state, not merely an absence. Muʿtazilites sometimes hold true and false assent to have one essential nature, with mere correspondence or noncorrespondence as an external condition. They cite the person who believes Zayd has remained inside all day although Zayd departed at noon: seemingly one continuous belief was knowledge in the morning, ignorance thereafter. The reply denies that matching reality is wholly irrelevant to the epistemic kind, and can deny the identity of successive beliefs: while Zayd was present, renewed convictions were knowledge; after his departure, renewed convictions were ignorance.

title: Potential, summary and detailed knowledge; necessary and acquired knowledge (I.230–233)
en:
### Potential, summary and detailed knowledge; necessary and acquired knowledge (I.230–233)

**“Third investigation: knowledge.”** Knowledge is either **eternal**, not preceded by nonexistence, namely God's knowledge, or **originated**, which belongs to creatures. Originated knowledge admits three stages. (1) **Pure potentiality**, readiness to know: outer and inner senses provide the material for necessary cognition, as touching a hot fire may dispose one to know that fire is hot; the premises of immediately known truths in turn dispose the mind to acquire demonstrative conclusions. (2) **Summary knowledge** (*ʿilm ijmālī*): someone who once mastered a question, then ceased to attend to it, can produce the answer immediately when asked. This is a simple undifferentiated state from which the articulated elements proceed. (3) **Detailed knowledge** (*ʿilm tafṣīlī*): the composite representation is present with its parts **individually distinguished and attended to**. We can glance at a written page and perceive it as a whole, then scrutinize individual characters one by one: these are analogous to summary and detailed awareness. Hence knowing a composite quiddity implies knowledge of its parts at least **in summary**.

Al-Rāzī objects that the one summary form, if single, would have to equal multiple essentially different quiddities; if it already contains separate forms for each, detailed knowledge exists. Simultaneous as opposed to successive presentation of those forms does not make a genuine middle stage between potentiality and full actuality. A possible answer distinguishes **one representation corresponding to the whole without explicit regard to the distinctions** from several representations referring to the parts separately. A different interpretation makes summary knowledge simply the mind's distinguishing a thing, and detailed knowledge the further awareness **that it distinguishes**; this risks reopening the disputes over whether knowing a thing entails knowing one's knowing it, and whether knowledge reflexively entails an actual infinity of higher-order acts.

**“Fourth investigation.”** Can necessary or immediate knowledge become knowledge requiring acquisition, and conversely? Al-Rāzī argues it cannot change either way, since whether understanding subject and predicate suffices for firm assent is an **essential** feature of a proposition; what is essential cannot be transformed. Yet his starting assumption needs proof, and is at most pertinent to first principles. Al-Āmidī and others allow, in principle, **inferential knowledge to become necessary**, for God could immediately create awareness of a truth previously reached through demonstration. Muʿtazilites support possibility by sameness of the generic nature of knowledge, but deny this occurs in obligated knowledge of God and His attributes, since it would undermine the obligation of acquiring it and allegedly impose what is not within human power. They treat this as an **external impediment to occurrence**, not an impossibility derived from knowledge's nature.

Al-Qāḍī and certain theologians also permit **necessary knowledge becoming acquired**, arguing that acts of knowledge share one essential nature and differ through their objects and individuating circumstances. An objection points out that **conception and assent** differ essentially. One can restrict the claim to knowledge as a species of assent, or maintain sameness within conceptions and separately within judgments, or appeal to a broad definition of knowledge as a quality producing discernment. Even if sameness is conceded, however, it does not follow that all externally conditioned possibilities of one instance hold for another: circumstances can render a transformation impossible, though it is unobjectionable to call each possible *considered simply as knowledge*. Al-Āmidī's appeal to differences in species or individuality seems to take the theologians' **tajāناس** as sharing merely a philosophical *genus*, overlooking their convention by which the relevant knowledges are **alike in species**.

Most deny that necessary cognition could become acquired: if it did, a competent mind attending to the object under the proper conditions could remain without it, a feature of acquired cognition. But the appeal to our experience of irresistibly possessing certain truths establishes **actual regularity**, not straightforward metaphysical impossibility; after transformation the former knowledge no longer possesses the relevant property. Al-Juwaynī, in one opinion also held by al-Qāḍī, exempts from transformation those necessities **required for perfection of the rational faculty** by which acquired knowledge itself becomes possible; if those became acquired, each would presuppose itself. This does not rule out transformation of **each necessary cognition considered individually**, provided not all the requisite first principles disappear together.

There is also debate whether a necessary judgment can **depend upon inferential knowledge**. One side says that if it depended on inquiry it would, by definition, be acquired. The other appeals to our necessary knowledge that contraries cannot coexist and claims we must first know of the contraries' existence. The better reply denies that judgment of impossibility requires a prior demonstrated knowledge of their **existence**: conceiving the two contraries in a suitable way suffices. Sometimes the **terms** of a judgment require investigation even though the inference to their relation is immediate. Whether that makes the judgment “necessary” may be verbal: does necessity mean no inquiry whatever, or no **demonstrative inference yielding the assent itself**? The theologians chiefly mean the latter. The real question is whether a noninferential assent can be grounded in separately inferred premises.

“Third investigation: knowledge.” Knowledge is either eternal, not preceded by nonexistence, namely God's knowledge, or originated, which belongs to creatures. Originated knowledge admits three stages. (1) Pure potentiality, readiness to know: outer and inner senses provide the material for necessary cognition, as touching a hot fire may dispose one to know that fire is hot; the premises of immediately known truths in turn dispose the mind to acquire demonstrative conclusions. (2) Summary knowledge (ʿilm ijmālī): someone who once mastered a question, then ceased to attend to it, can produce the answer immediately when asked. This is a simple undifferentiated state from which the articulated elements proceed. (3) Detailed knowledge (ʿilm tafṣīlī): the composite representation is present with its parts individually distinguished and attended to. We can glance at a written page and perceive it as a whole, then scrutinize individual characters one by one: these are analogous to summary and detailed awareness. Hence knowing a composite quiddity implies knowledge of its parts at least in summary.

Al-Rāzī objects that the one summary form, if single, would have to equal multiple essentially different quiddities; if it already contains separate forms for each, detailed knowledge exists. Simultaneous as opposed to successive presentation of those forms does not make a genuine middle stage between potentiality and full actuality. A possible answer distinguishes one representation corresponding to the whole without explicit regard to the distinctions from several representations referring to the parts separately. A different interpretation makes summary knowledge simply the mind's distinguishing a thing, and detailed knowledge the further awareness that it distinguishes; this risks reopening the disputes over whether knowing a thing entails knowing one's knowing it, and whether knowledge reflexively entails an actual infinity of higher-order acts.

“Fourth investigation.” Can necessary or immediate knowledge become knowledge requiring acquisition, and conversely? Al-Rāzī argues it cannot change either way, since whether understanding subject and predicate suffices for firm assent is an essential feature of a proposition; what is essential cannot be transformed. Yet his starting assumption needs proof, and is at most pertinent to first principles. Al-Āmidī and others allow, in principle, inferential knowledge to become necessary, for God could immediately create awareness of a truth previously reached through demonstration. Muʿtazilites support possibility by sameness of the generic nature of knowledge, but deny this occurs in obligated knowledge of God and His attributes, since it would undermine the obligation of acquiring it and allegedly impose what is not within human power. They treat this as an external impediment to occurrence, not an impossibility derived from knowledge's nature.

Al-Qāḍī and certain theologians also permit necessary knowledge becoming acquired, arguing that acts of knowledge share one essential nature and differ through their objects and individuating circumstances. An objection points out that conception and assent differ essentially. One can restrict the claim to knowledge as a species of assent, or maintain sameness within conceptions and separately within judgments, or appeal to a broad definition of knowledge as a quality producing discernment. Even if sameness is conceded, however, it does not follow that all externally conditioned possibilities of one instance hold for another: circumstances can render a transformation impossible, though it is unobjectionable to call each possible considered simply as knowledge. Al-Āmidī's appeal to differences in species or individuality seems to take the theologians' tajāناس as sharing merely a philosophical genus, overlooking their convention by which the relevant knowledges are alike in species.

Most deny that necessary cognition could become acquired: if it did, a competent mind attending to the object under the proper conditions could remain without it, a feature of acquired cognition. But the appeal to our experience of irresistibly possessing certain truths establishes actual regularity, not straightforward metaphysical impossibility; after transformation the former knowledge no longer possesses the relevant property. Al-Juwaynī, in one opinion also held by al-Qāḍī, exempts from transformation those necessities required for perfection of the rational faculty by which acquired knowledge itself becomes possible; if those became acquired, each would presuppose itself. This does not rule out transformation of each necessary cognition considered individually, provided not all the requisite first principles disappear together.

There is also debate whether a necessary judgment can depend upon inferential knowledge. One side says that if it depended on inquiry it would, by definition, be acquired. The other appeals to our necessary knowledge that contraries cannot coexist and claims we must first know of the contraries' existence. The better reply denies that judgment of impossibility requires a prior demonstrated knowledge of their existence: conceiving the two contraries in a suitable way suffices. Sometimes the terms of a judgment require investigation even though the inference to their relation is immediate. Whether that makes the judgment “necessary” may be verbal: does necessity mean no inquiry whatever, or no demonstrative inference yielding the assent itself? The theologians chiefly mean the latter. The real question is whether a noninferential assent can be grounded in separately inferred premises.

title: Whether one knowledge apprehends many objects; the seat of knowledge (I.233–235)
en:
### Whether one knowledge apprehends many objects; the seat of knowledge (I.233–235)

**“Fifth investigation.”** Those who affirm eternal knowledge agree that it is **one divine knowledge with numerous objects**. They dispute originated knowledge: al-Ashʿarī and many Muʿtazilites prohibit one originated knowledge from having two distinct objects, whence the formula that knowledge multiplies with its objects; others allow one knowledge with multiple objects. Al-Rāzī associates the disagreement with the definition of knowledge: if knowledge is purely **relation**, its several attachments are themselves several knowledges; if it is a **quality having relations**, one quality can have many attachments, as in the case of divine knowledge. The disagreement concerns knowing **many things distinctly and as many**; knowing a composite as a whole without analysis is not a relevant counterexample.

The logical possibility of a relational quality with several objects does not alone establish its extramental possibility. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Bāhilī denies shared knowledge in the case of two inferred truths, since demonstrations of the Maker's existence and of His unity are different. The reply denies that **one inquiry** cannot produce more than one cognition: one demonstration may make known its conclusion, the absence of a decisive counterargument, and that the resulting state is knowledge rather than ignorance. Al-Qāḍī and al-Juwaynī deny one knowledge of two objects when knowledge of one could **come apart from** knowledge of the other, arguing that the one knowledge would then separate from itself. The reply distinguishes their **general separability**, since two different knowledges can be had, from their **simultaneous inseparability under a particular common cognition**. The possibility of separation remains in itself, but the posited single cognition can impose an external impossibility of separating it into two. Defining the objects as such that their cognitions can never under any circumstances coincide begs the question.

A further argument says that if one quality generated two different qualifications—knowing black and knowing white—it could equally generate **knowing and being-powerful**, collapsing all attributes into one. But these cases are not alike: the two qualifications of knowing are homogeneous, unlike knowledge and power. For inseparable contents such as adjacency, likeness or opposition, one act might necessarily know both terms. A challenge from **reflexive knowledge** is that knowing any thing necessarily entails knowing that one knows it, then knowledge of that knowledge ad infinitum; if every content needed a separate act this would produce an actual infinity of cognitions. The reply denies the universal entailment of actual attention to one's own knowledge; alternatively higher-order awareness can be merely **conceptual differentiation**, terminating whenever consideration ceases.

**Source-critical warning at printed p.234.** Both the saved OpenITI transcription and a separately consulted online reading of this printed page contain an **intrusive paragraph from the earlier discussion of time and from the subsequent discussion of bodies**, inserted abruptly after “if some of these known things were not known by one knowledge.” This interrupts the sentence before the text resumes on p.235 with “... there would have to be infinitely many cognitions in every person who knew anything.” This is not a doctrinal excursus and has been **excluded from the translated argument**, but the electronic Arabic source is retained literally to permit collation. The editorial issue must be resolved from a scanned printed witness before a definitive edition.

**“Then concerning multiplicity [of knowledges].”** Two distinct cognitions can concern one object; whether they are **of the same kind** requires distinguishing the subject (*maḥall*) of knowledge, the knower, and its object (*mutaʿallaq*). Where the knowers differ, as when Zayd and ʿAmr both know the Maker's eternity, the cognitions are different if inherence in each subject individuates the knowledge essentially; otherwise they may be alike. When the objects differ, two cognitions are different whether they are of two white things or of white and black. When the object is one, the majority regard the cognitions as alike even if the objects are known under different temporal descriptions. Al-Āmidī rightly objects that “Zayd stands now” and “Zayd stands tomorrow” have **different propositional contents** because the time belongs to what is judged, unlike two acts of knowing the **same thing at different times**. Al-Taftāzānī accepts this correction: variation in the **time predicated of the object** makes the object of cognition different; genuine sameness of object with multiplicity of knowledge may involve different times **of the knowing** or different subjects.

**“Sixth investigation.”** Qurʾān and transmitted reports associate originated knowledge with the **heart**. Reason does not compel knowledge to inhere only there: God could create it in any substance. Many investigators understand “heart” not as the anatomical organ common to animals but as the **spirit distinguishing the human being**. The philosophers commonly locate universal knowledge in the immaterial rational soul, while sensible particulars are registered in outward and inward faculties; their more penetrating account assigns **all cognition to the soul**, with universals apprehended immediately and particulars through bodily instruments. A fuller examination belongs to the treatment of the soul.

title: Reason as a condition of obligation; the definition of will (I.235)
en:
### Reason as a condition of obligation; the definition of will (I.235)

**“Seventh investigation.”** All agree that the **rational faculty** (*ʿaql*) is the condition under which religious obligations bind, and hence that children lacking it, the insane and nonrational animals are not addressed by such obligations. Since “intellect” has many meanings, al-Ashʿarī takes it here as **knowledge of some immediate, universal, self-evident truths**, enabling acquisition of theoretical conclusions. If intellect were a different thing from knowledge, one might expect an intelligent person without knowledge or a knower without intellect. If it were knowledge of inferred conclusions, those conclusions would depend upon intellect and intellect would thus presuppose itself. If it required **every** necessary truth, a person missing one because of lack of attention, experience or transmitted confirmation would no longer be rational, contrary to agreement.

The first argument is challenged: really distinct things may be inseparable, so conceptual nonidentity does not entail possible separation. The claim that a reasoner cannot exist without knowing, or a knower without reason, is disputed in sleep. The preferable account describes reason as **a power accompanying sufficient first principles**, permitting inferential acquisition. This is close to al-Rāzī's account of a **disposition** (*gharīza*) from which immediate knowledge follows given sound faculties; to a capacity for distinguishing good from bad; and to the uṣūlī definition of a **light illuminating a road beginning where sense-perception terminates**. In each formulation an intellectual ability arises with the grasp of particulars and prepares for theoretical knowledge. It corresponds to philosophers' **intellect in possession** (*ʿaql bi-l-malaka*).

**Electronic witness anomaly.** The middle of printed page 235 in the preserved online text abruptly inserts alien material on infinite magnitudes, parallelism, dimensional finitude and directions, ending with a page marker from p.325. This portion is manifestly out of place in the discussion of intellect; the translation resumes at “like a substance with an accident, and a cause with an effect.” It is preserved in the Arabic source, **not adopted as part of al-Taftāzānī's argument about ʿaql**. A critical Arabic reconstruction requires consultation of a printed scan.

**“And among [psychological qualities] is will.”** The meaning of **will** (*irāda*) seems intuitively distinguishable from other states although its essence resists exact definition. It is not **appetite or desire** (*shahwa*), as aversion of will (*karāha*) is not sheer natural repulsion (*nufra*). One may will to drink an unpleasant but salutary medicine without appetitive desire, and desire a delicious but harmful dish without willing to eat it. Many Muʿtazilites identify will with **belief or presumption of benefit**: power by itself is equally related to acting and refraining, while a belief favouring one side makes it prevail. Others require an additional **inclination** following the belief, since apparent benefit may be judged without willing it. The first group replies that the relevant belief is in **accessible benefit to oneself or someone one cares about**, unimpeded by weariness or opposing reasons, while yearning for an inaccessible beloved exemplifies the inclination proper to **imperfect power**, not a universal condition of will.

title: Irāda, appetite, desire, and whether willing implies aversion to the opposite (I.236–237)
en:
### Irāda, appetite, desire, and whether willing implies aversion to the opposite (I.236–237)

**The Ashʿarite objection to reducing will to benefit-belief.** A freely choosing subject, we hold, can select **one of two exactly equal alternatives** by will alone, without discovering or believing some special benefit in that alternative. Muʿtazilites claim immediate awareness that every choice needs a distinguishing motive, and argue that a choice between truly equal alternatives may in fact be impossible even when the hypothetical is easy to imagine. Ashʿarites counter that awareness supports **the efficacy of will itself**, independent of differential advantage. Will may therefore be defined as an attribute by which a subject specifies one among its two possible outcomes—**doing or omitting**. Defining the attribute by this effect does not prove that its intrinsic nature differs from belief or inclination; neither does it force all its objects to be what the agent can produce. We can will **life** or **death**, or will to **will something** or to **dislike something**. Wishing to dislike what one otherwise desires does not amount to both willing and disliking the **same** thing under one description. Appetite, by contrast, cannot simply have appetite itself as object in the same way: “I wish to wish,” spoken by a sick person, really means a **volition** for appetite's restoration.

**The philosophers.** They deny that the Necessary Being acts through a deliberative, alternative-selecting will, regarding Him as necessitating by essence. To avoid attributing His action to the unknowing mode of inert nature they call Him *willing* by identifying divine will with **knowledge of the good and perfection as good**, or the knowledge of one's own act which produces the act without external compulsion or constraint. An objection notes that if all will is cognition it could occur only in cognitive beings, whereas **voluntary motion** enters the definition of animal as such. The philosophers distinguish the **common animal sense of will**, namely appetitive inclination towards or away from action, from what can be predicated of God.

**“Second investigation.”** Al-Ashʿarī and his followers identify **willing something** with **disliking its contrary**. If the two were distinct, they must supposedly be alike, contrary, or disparate. They cannot be alike or contrary, since willing one thing and rejecting its contrary coexist; if disparate, each should be able to coexist with the other's opposite, allowing willing both contraries. Several steps are disputed. Not being identical does not necessarily establish the stipulated mode of otherness, and even disparate qualities may have relations of **entailment** preventing combinations: what entails a given state cannot coexist with its opposite. Or both may be opposed to a third state, as different kinds of uncertain assent are opposed to knowledge. More fundamentally, willing something necessarily involves **awareness of what one wills**, but one often wills it without considering its opposite, so cannot thereby dislike the opposite under a conscious description. Conditioning identity on having thought about the opposite does not repair the claim of identity: a thing cannot be itself only **on condition** that another cognition occurs.

Al-Qāḍī and al-Ghazālī, while accepting difference of states, affirm an **entailment** between willing an object and disliking its *consciously considered* contrary. Otherwise, the contrary might also be willed and two contrary volitions would coexist. The premises are challengeable: one can consider an alternative without either willing or rejecting it, and two contraries may each be desired under **different respects**, possibly with different strengths. Conversely the proposed entailment seems to imply that disliking a thing requires willing its contrary, generating contradictions when one has multiple contraries. Qualifying the claim by **respects** or by a unique contrary may avoid that formulation. An attempt to exclude willing opposed future events by insisting will can concern only one's present act conflicts with **ordinary usage**; willing another person's action or a future act is not invariably mere wishful thinking. The precise distinction must be formulated without assuming from the outset that the object of every human will is both presently produced and immediately simultaneous with the volition.

title: The nature of power, effective causation, and the Ashʿarite account (I.237–239)
en:
### The nature of power, effective causation, and the Ashʿarite account (I.237–239)

**“Among them is power (*qudra*).”** “Strength” (*quwwa*) may mean the ability of a living being to perform arduous tasks, opposed to weakness; or it may refer to an **effective principle** (*mabdaʾ al-taghayyur*), a source of change in another **qua other**. The latter phrase distinguishes producer from patient. The qualifier *qua other* allows them to be one in subject but two in respect, as a physician treating himself: physician as possessor of medical knowledge, patient as a body affected by medication. More exactly, the intellective soul is what directs and the body what receives. The mutuality is especially clear if a physician improves his own character. The definition of power in terms of effects should be understood as **aptitude to act**, not necessarily actually causing an effect at every moment.

Al-Āmidī accordingly describes power as a **positive attribute of a subject** such that through it production and origination are open to that subject, with **acting rather than omitting, and omitting rather than acting**, conceived as available alternatives. On Ashʿarite principles originated power is present in creatures, although an action's actual creation belongs to God. The fact that this power does not itself create in the Muʿtazilite sense does not abolish power: a capacity may fail to realize its inherent operation owing to an impediment. Hence one need not choose between the unrestricted Muʿtazilite doctrine that humans create by their powers and Jahm ibn Ṣafwān's complete denial of human power. The experienced differences between involuntary trembling and intentional striking, ascending and descending, remain intact. Whether a power **without actual production** should still be named *power* is partly verbal; divine eternal power with temporally originated objects and the Muʿtazilite idea of human power preceding action both exhibit the same conceptual separation of capacity from present effect.

**“Immediate awareness testifies.”** The Ashʿarite ground for recognizing human power is **direct experience**: one finds oneself able to initiate or withhold an intentional blow in a way one does not command involuntary shaking. This is better than inferring power merely from different people's successful and unsuccessful acts, since an external prohibition can frustrate someone who possesses the power. The obstructed person remains intrinsically unchanged when the prohibition is removed; this differs from a person whose actual **incapacity** must itself be removed. Nor is power identical with healthy bodily constitution or mere freedom from disease: a sleeping healthy person is not presently capable in the required sense. Direct experience distinguishes power from sensible temperament, the mere integrity of organs, and **bodily members**; it is not simply the healthy hand that strikes or healthy leg that walks, despite reports attributing that view to Ḍirār and Hishām. If the claim “power is part of the powerful subject” means only that power is an **attribute inhering in it**, that is the majority view; if “power is part of the possible act” means the act's *being possible for the agent*, it uses **power** in the derivative sense of *maqduriyya*.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir identifies power with **bodily soundness**, and al-Rāzī is drawn to the view. The critics answer that two equally sound subjects differ in their ability to write, or the same subject reads but cannot write; an additional specification is required. Al-Rāzī challenges the alleged freedom to do or not do: before the action, an action not occurring is impossible under the actual conditions; during the action its omission is impossible; when God creates the movement it occurs necessarily, and before creation it cannot occur; when motives are equal action cannot be selected, while when motives differ only the stronger side prevails. The Ashʿarite reply distinguishes **the alternative-act structure considered through the power itself** from **the necessity or impossibility arising through additional considerations**—whether the action is stipulated to exist or not, whether God has created it, and whether some motive prevails. In the first respect intentional movement differs essentially in experience from involuntary trembling, even if its total conditions decisively determine occurrence in the second respect.

The fact that this power does not itself create in the Muʿtazilite sense does not abolish power: a capacity may fail to realize its inherent operation owing to an impediment. Hence one need not choose between the unrestricted Muʿtazilite doctrine that humans create by their powers and Jahm ibn Ṣafwān's complete denial of human power. The experienced differences between involuntary trembling and intentional striking, ascending and descending, remain intact. Whether a power without actual production should still be named power is partly verbal; divine eternal power with temporally originated objects and the Muʿtazilite idea of human power preceding action both exhibit the same conceptual separation of capacity from present effect.

“Immediate awareness testifies.” The Ashʿarite ground for recognizing human power is direct experience: one finds oneself able to initiate or withhold an intentional blow in a way one does not command involuntary shaking. This is better than inferring power merely from different people's successful and unsuccessful acts, since an external prohibition can frustrate someone who possesses the power. The obstructed person remains intrinsically unchanged when the prohibition is removed; this differs from a person whose actual incapacity must itself be removed. Nor is power identical with healthy bodily constitution or mere freedom from disease: a sleeping healthy person is not presently capable in the required sense. Direct experience distinguishes power from sensible temperament, the mere integrity of organs, and bodily members; it is not simply the healthy hand that strikes or healthy leg that walks, despite reports attributing that view to Ḍirār and Hishām. If the claim “power is part of the powerful subject” means only that power is an attribute inhering in it, that is the majority view; if “power is part of the possible act” means the act's being possible for the agent, it uses power in the derivative sense of maqduriyya.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir identifies power with bodily soundness, and al-Rāzī is drawn to the view. The critics answer that two equally sound subjects differ in their ability to write, or the same subject reads but cannot write; an additional specification is required. Al-Rāzī challenges the alleged freedom to do or not do: before the action, an action not occurring is impossible under the actual conditions; during the action its omission is impossible; when God creates the movement it occurs necessarily, and before creation it cannot occur; when motives are equal action cannot be selected, while when motives differ only the stronger side prevails. The Ashʿarite reply distinguishes the alternative-act structure considered through the power itself from the necessity or impossibility arising through additional considerations—whether the action is stipulated to exist or not, whether God has created it, and whether some motive prevails. In the first respect intentional movement differs essentially in experience from involuntary trembling, even if its total conditions decisively determine occurrence in the second respect.

title: Is originated power simultaneous with action or prior to it? (I.239–240)
en:
### Is originated power simultaneous with action or prior to it? (I.239–240)

**“Second investigation.”** Does *istiṭāʿa*, an originated agent's ability, exist **before** its act or **with** it? Ashʿarites and several Sunni theologians defend simultaneity; most Muʿtazilites affirm precedence, then dispute whether that power necessarily persists at the moment of action.

Ashʿarite proofs include: (1) power is an **accident**; on the atomistic premise that accidents cannot persist through two instants, if it existed earlier it would vanish before the act, allegedly leaving an effect without its cause. Eternal divine power is not an accident. A response distinguishes the impossibility of an effect **without any cause** from the disputed possibility of an effect whose source was **earlier but not simultaneous**. Alternatively, similar powers can be continually recreated across instants, as happens with knowledge, inclination and expectation, all of which can precede their objects. The last reply is incomplete: if the act occurs by the disappeared power, the original problem returns, while if it occurs by the newly originated simultaneous power, that is precisely the Ashʿarite thesis. The original reasoning in any event is an argument **against those who ascribe real production to human power**.

(2) While an act **does not exist**, it is impossible, since existence and nonexistence cannot coexist; but an impossible object is admittedly beyond power. (3) If power were present beforehand, the act beforehand would be possible; yet stipulating its occurrence then would make power simultaneous instead of earlier. These two arguments conflate modalities. An action **while stipulated nonexistent** cannot simultaneously be existent, but this does not mean it cannot instead exist **at that very time**, the nonexistence then failing to obtain. Standing is incompatible with **continuing to sit**, but is certainly possible **at a time when someone actually sits**, in the sense that sitting might cease and standing replace it. The arguments also risk counting against **divine eternal power** unless the qualifications are carefully distinguished.

Muʿtazilites offer objections to simultaneity. (1) If power relates to the act only at its occurrence, power seems to **produce an already existing thing**, the acquisition of what has already been obtained. (2) The whole notion of **obligation** collapses: one is commanded **before acting**, but if one then lacks power to act, every actual religious obligation would command what cannot be done, contrary even to those who theoretically allow some impossible commands. (3) Since God's power is eternal, if power and act are invariably simultaneous, all actual products of divine power must be eternal. To (1) the reply distinguishes an act existing **through this very act of creation** from one existing independently prior to it: only the latter would be produced twice. To (2) the defender does not require already actual power at the moment of receiving the command, only that the act be of a kind the subject can perform, unlike **creating bodies**. A related account requires that either the commanded act or its opposite fall within the scope of human power, and the unbeliever's withholding belief differs in this regard from inability to create substances. To (3) the reply distinguishes an **eternal capacity itself** from its temporally particular **relation or effectuation**; its relation to a created act can be originated without making the eternal quality originated or its temporal object eternal.

Al-Āmidī's argument can be understood as saying divine power relates **in the sense of creating** when the temporal act is possible and originates, not in eternity when the act would have to be eternal. But “attachment” is equivocal: if it means a **relation enabling one to say the agent is presently capable**, its temporal status follows the power itself, whereas if it denotes the actual **production of the effect**, it is indeed simultaneous with production. Confusing those meanings makes apparent objections against both parties easier than substantive resolution.

title: Consequences of simultaneity; one power and several possible acts (I.241–242)
en:
### Consequences of simultaneity; one power and several possible acts (I.241–242)

**“Consequently, on the view that power accompanies action, the obstructed person...”** An agent presently prevented from an act he might otherwise perform is not capable **at the moment of prevention** in the strict Ashʿarite sense, any more than a person paralysed by incapacity, although the causes of their inability differ. Moreover, one simultaneous power cannot be related to **two actual objects**, whether contrary, similar or merely different, because the power present at the issuance of one act differs from the power present at another. An objection distinguishes differences in **relational descriptions**—being able to do this rather than that—from differences in the intrinsic power itself. If “power” includes both a shared ability and whatever makes the relation specific, it becomes equivocal, which neither side normally acknowledges.

The Muʿtazilites argue that an obstructed agent remains **capable**; the hindrance prevents **the act**, not the power. Hindrance may be absence of a condition, an existing contrary such as stillness opposed to motion, or a factor that itself generates a contrary effect, such as heaviness preventing upward movement. We immediately distinguish a **bound person** unable to walk from a **paralysed person** unable to walk. The bound person has not necessarily suffered a change in his intrinsic properties, nor acquired a contrary of power. The Ashʿarite rejoinder attributes the difference to **regular divine custom**: removal of restraint is normally followed by creation of power in the bound person, but this is not the ordinary course for the paralysed person. The denial that restraint leaves the person's relevant power intrinsically intact may also be contested.

Muʿtazilites agree that one power can reach **similar acts at different times**, though not simultaneous numerically similar events in one subject under the same power. They dispute whether one power may extend to **contraries**. Most permit alternatives: without capacity to omit an act, the agent would be necessitated rather than free. Abū Hāshim proposes several accounts. He sometimes distinguishes powers inhering in the **heart** from those in the **limbs**, each relating to all possible acts in its own locus; sometimes grants each relation to both classes but actual efficacy only in its own seat through the presence of appropriate conditions; sometimes differentiates the range of the two powers asymmetrically; and sometimes gives heart-power a wider relational range, although it does not produce bodily acts, while denying limb-power any relation to acts of the heart. The short *matn* alludes to the last two possibilities.

Al-Rāzī proposes a reconciliation by clarifying “power.” If it means **the fundamental causal aptitude** underlying different acts, irrespective of whether all conditions are complete, then it naturally exists before, with and after individual exercises and may concern contraries. If it means the power **together with every condition for producing this particular act**, then it exists simultaneously with that act and cannot concern its contrary, for the complete actualizing conditions differ. Since al-Ashʿarī denies that human originated power creates in the strict sense, “efficacy” here must include **acquisition (*kasb*)**, i.e. the completion of conditions under which divine custom produces an act. A basic aptitude before action and a completed conjunction simultaneous with it need not be mutually exclusive doctrines when their subjects are distinguished.

title: Incapacity, character, pleasure and pain (I.242–244)
en:
### Incapacity, character, pleasure and pain (I.242–244)

**“Third investigation.”** The majority call **incapacity** (*ʿajz*) a positive accident **contrary** to power, since, they say, a paralysed person has a distinct state absent from a merely obstructed person, though neither is presently able to act. Abū Hāshim instead treats incapacity as **privation of power**, with no separate opposite accident inhering in the paralysed. From the theory of a positive contrary al-Ashʿarī draws the conclusion that incapacity, like power, must relate only to **what exists**; the paralysed person, he says, is incapable of the **existing sitting**, not the absent standing. Al-Taftāzānī calls this untenable: even if incapacity is positive, its relation to nonexistents is no more inconceivable than that of knowledge or volition to a nonactual object. Our everyday judgment that someone is incapable of **producing a counterpart of the Qurʾān**, not incapable of remaining silent, illustrates this. Redefining one “incapacity” as an absence directed to a nonexistent and another as a positive quality relating only to a present act is not normal linguistic usage.

Does **sleep** exclude power? A sleeper can sometimes act, but cannot perform most deliberate activities. Muʿtazilites and some Ashʿarites allow the relevant acts to be within a sleeper's power; Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī likens sleep to the absence of cognition and denies power; al-Qāḍī and others suspend judgment. Numerous derivative Muʿtazilite distinctions are passed over.

**“Character (*khuluq*) is opposed to it [power].”** A character trait is a **settled disposition** from which acts proceed **with ease and without preceding deliberation**. A transient anger in a normally patient person is not a character trait. Nor does every stable ability count: writing skill yields easily produced **bodily acts**, while power is equally ordered to doing and refraining; a miser may give generously only through difficult reflection, while a generous person may give for calculated public prestige. Character is distinguished from power because power is not defined by ease or independence from deliberation, and is indifferent between act and omission. This is the sense of the *Tajrīd* statement that their opposed consequences mark a contrary relation.

**“Pleasure and pain.”** Their experiential meanings are evident, so philosophical formulas identify their referents rather than establishing a strict definition. **Pleasure** is apprehending what is fitting *as fitting*; **pain** is apprehending what is adverse *as adverse*. The fitting is the appropriate perfection of a faculty: sweetness to taste, or correct intelligible objects to intellect. The qualification **“as fitting”** matters because a person with a bodily condition may not enjoy a thing typically agreeable to taste. Apprehension must also signify **actual attainment**, not merely entertaining an image. Imagining a pleasant object does not provide the same pleasure as obtaining it. Avicenna therefore more precisely speaks of **apprehending and attaining the arrival of** what appears perfection and good to the perceiver, or harmful and evil in the case of pain. The thing's presence **to the one enjoying it** is required, not merely the representation of something pleasant. **Perfection** means the actualization of the capacity belonging to the subject; **good** means what the subject favours or prefers. The subject's understanding of something as fitting may differ from its actual objective benefit; hence the same object can be pleasurable to one person, painful to another.

Al-Rāzī doubts whether pleasure is **identical with** the apprehension of the agreeable, a separate state caused by it, or something that can occur in another way. He also doubts that pain simply equals awareness of the adverse: physicians observe a gradually established moist disturbance that is abnormal yet not painful. Muḥammad ibn Zakariyyāʾ al-Rāzī and Galen define pleasure instead as **a return from an abnormal state to a normal one**, or the release from pain, as hunger relieved by eating. Avicenna objects that pleasures can occur **without preceding discomfort**, as in unexpectedly acquiring wealth, perceiving beauty never desired, or first tasting sweetness; recovery to health can also occur gradually **without pleasure**, and agreeable sensations can go unnoticed when attention is otherwise engaged. The Galenic account may mistake an **accidental concomitant** of many sensory pleasures for their intrinsic nature: because changes in the bodily organ are often needed to generate sensory discrimination, pleasure frequently accompanies transition. Yet this alone does not show pleasure **is** the transition, and the dispute cannot be dismissed without considering counterexamples on both sides.

title: Intellectual pleasure and the medical causes of pain (I.244–245)
en:
### Intellectual pleasure and the medical causes of pain (I.244–245)

**“Both pleasure and pain divide into sensory and intellectual kinds.”** Bodily enjoyment appears in taste and other sensory faculties, while anger and estimation also involve satisfaction when anticipating victory or a hoped-for outcome. There is an **intellectual perfection**: the rational substance represents, as far as possible, the Necessary Being and the ordered intelligible effects deriving from Him, so that the whole order of existence is apprehended accurately, purified of confused guesses and imaginings—an attained intellect (*ʿaql mustafād*). To apprehend and attain such perfection is **intellectual pleasure**; to experience its contrary as a deprivation is intellectual pain. Intellectual pleasure is greater in **extent**, since intelligibles are far more numerous and virtually inexhaustible, and in **degree**, since intellect reaches the essences of intelligibles whereas sense attends chiefly to bodily surfaces. Why, then, do scholars sometimes fail to enjoy their knowledge or suffer from ignorance? They may lack the requisite attention, attainment or other conditions for pleasure. Sensory pleasure need not be classified merely as sensible quality, because the **sensible taste or warmth** is one thing and the **enjoyment or suffering arising upon its perception** is another, apprehended by inward awareness.

**“Sensory pain, especially that of touch, is called *wajaʿ*.”** Ordinary language often reserves “pleasure” and “pain” for the sensory, although philosophical usage extends both to intellection by common meaning. “Ache” or “hurt” most properly refers to sensible, particularly tactile, pain. The physicians usually recognize just two broad causes of bodily pain: **disruption of continuity** (*tafarroq al-ittiṣāl*) and an **alien, discordant temperament** (*sūʾ al-mizāj al-mukhtalif*). A physiological argument starts from an organ's proper perfection—its balanced temperament and suitable form and structure. Either alteration of temperament or disruption of its structural continuity deprives it of this perfection. Disagreement concerns whether each causes pain **per se**, as Avicenna allows, or whether disruption alone is per se with temperament causing pain through disruption, the view often associated with Galen; or the reverse, that temperament alone is per se and disruption acts through it, preferred by al-Rāzī and later writers. Detailed counterarguments are left to commentaries on the *Qānūn*.

Avicenna confines painful **temperamental disturbance in itself** to **heat and cold** rather than moisture or dryness, and to **discordant rather than fully assimilated** temperament. His explanation that moisture and dryness are passive, not active qualities is questioned: dryness can disrupt tissue and cause disease, and both moisture and dryness are themselves tactile qualities. If they become excessive, why could their perception as hostile not be painful? Conversely there is no demonstration that heat, cold and disruption alone act as natural efficient causes of pain. Avicenna nevertheless allows dry temperament to produce pain **accidentally** through contraction and disrupted continuity. One could similarly contend that excessive wetness stretches tissue and disrupts it; the reply distinguishes **moisture with extraneous matter** causing pressure from moisture in itself.

An **assimilated alien temperament** does not hurt because, after gradual establishment in an organ, it functions like the organ's new normal condition: the sense no longer reacts to it. Pain requires an ongoing contrast between some retained normal state and the invading contrary. This explains why a severe prolonged fever, although hotter and more materially destructive than an acute intermittent fever, can feel less fiery, and why the body initially experiences tepid, then hot water as painful but gradually finds each agreeable, only to experience the earlier water as cold. A gradual change may pass unnoticed because each increment is too small to register against its immediately preceding state; sudden changes present a larger contrast and persist in awareness until habituation.

title: Objections to tissue disruption as a source of pain; the concept of health (I.246–248)
en:
### Objections to tissue disruption as a source of pain; the concept of health (I.246–248)

The theory that **disrupted continuity** causes pain faces several objections. (1) “Separation” is a **privation** of connection, but pain is positive; how could a privation produce it? The reply distinguishes **actual separation as movement of parts away from each other** from mere absence of connection. Even on a privative description, the organ's losing a fitting structure supplies the relevant object of adverse apprehension; and “cause” in medical language often means a **preparatory condition**, not the efficient creator of pain. (2) Every person continually undergoes microscopic bodily separation in **nutrition and metabolism**, so why are we not perpetually in pain? These processes may fall below threshold, remain familiar and beneficial, or not be apprehended **as harmful**. title: Disease, privation and contrariety; whether a third bodily condition exists (I.248–250)
en:
### Disease, privation and contrariety; whether a third bodily condition exists (I.248–250)

**“Disease”** is defined as a condition **contrary to health** in which the subject's functions proceed abnormally. Yet Avicenna elsewhere says that disease **qua disease** is an absence, rather than a positive disturbance, pain, or foreign temperament. These formulations can be reconciled if disease names either **the privation of the health-giving condition** or the **positive contrary quality** responsible for defective action. In the first sense it is opposed to health by **privation/possession**, in the second by **contrariety**. Another reconciliation distinguishes the widespread usage of “contrary” as two mutually exclusive descriptions—including rest versus movement—from strict Aristotelian contraries within a close genus. But if one insists on the strict division, the difficulty remains.

Al-Rāzī notes that physicians divide simple diseases into **bad temperament**, **faulty composition**, and **separation of continuity**. None appears to be a psychological quality of the genus habit or state. Bad temperament can be an actual **tactile quality** such as foreign heat, or the body's becoming affected by it; faulty composition may involve deficient magnitude, number, arrangement, shape, or blocked passages; separation is privative. These items span different categories, and the argument is not adequately represented by compressing them into a few alternative instances. The reply says the medical classification names disease by its **causal or differentiating conditions**, while the disease *as a psychological quality of the body* is a consequent state arising in conjunction with them. Thus one may casually call balanced temperament “health” even if the philosophical quality of health is not identical with the sensible balance itself.

**“Then the relevant consideration.”** Is there a **middle condition between health and disease**? The question is not whether there are countless other states—knowledge, life, power—to which neither predicate is essentially assigned. It asks whether a given body or organ at a given time may **actually be neither healthy nor diseased**. Galen accepts a third bodily state, illustrated by people recovering from illness, older people, children, and organisms with some sound and some diseased organs. Avicenna objects that logical comparisons must hold fixed **one subject, one time, the same bodily part, and the same respect**. For this fixed subject, if disease simply means **failure to possess the condition giving all the relevant functions their normal soundness**, a middle is excluded: the condition either holds or does not. If instead disease means **all functions are defective**, a genuine middle is obvious where **some functions are sound and some defective**. A still wider sense—every bodily organ healthy versus every organ diseased—makes middle cases common. Al-Rāzī accordingly treats much of the dispute as **verbal**, dependent on how comprehensive the predicates are. Avicenna criticizes definitions of health that attach unnecessary conditions such as perfect functioning **of every organ, at every time, and without vulnerability to imminent relapse**; these would artificially exclude children, the elderly and convalescents from the predicate “healthy.”

title: Emotions, shape and angle as quantities or qualities (I.250–253)
en:
### Emotions, shape and angle as quantities or qualities (I.250–253)

**“Among them is joy.”** Psychological states arise following perceptions of what benefits or harms the subject. The traditional physiological accounts assign different motions of the animal spirit to them. **Joy** is associated with outward expansion to obtain what delights; **distress** with inward contraction at an experienced evil; **anger** with outward movement seeking revenge; **terror** with inward flight from actual or imagined injury; **sorrow** with slowly progressive inward contraction; **anxiety** with alternating inward and outward movements because some impending event presents both hoped-for benefit and feared harm. Since attention moves between the two, anxiety is also called **mental struggle**. **Shame** may begin with frightened contraction and end with modest outward relief on recognizing that the threat is smaller than first supposed. These descriptions name **effects and signs**, not strict essences. Everyday language also loosely calls joy expansion of the heart, distress contraction, or anger a boiling of the blood.

**“Third class: qualities peculiar to quantities.”** Such qualities primarily attach to **continuous quantity**, like straightness and curvature of lines or concavity and convexity of surfaces, and to **discrete quantity**, like parity and oddness of numbers. A physical body is straight, curved or even-numbered only by means of its quantitative aspects. Some include **shape/figure** (*khalqa*) as a composite of **form (*shakl*) and colour**. Three objections arise. First, colour is a sensible quality, seemingly opposed to quantity-peculiar qualities. One reply treats colour as primarily a property of the **surface**, so the categories need not be mutually exclusive; still it is plausible that colouring may permeate a body's depth. Second, the proposed genus should contain **single qualities**, not arbitrary composites of several; why single out form-and-colour rather than infinite combinations? Their particular conjunction allegedly determines beauty or ugliness, giving the composite a special character. Third, *khalqa* seems to require a natural body, whereas pure geometrical qualities can be grasped without bodily matter. The distinction is that some properties accrue to **quantity as such**, the subject of mathematics, while others arise as properties of **quantities of special kinds of bodies**. Furthermore “figure” may mean the sum of colour and form, or form in association with colour, or a **new quality resulting from their conjunction**; the last is more plausible if counted as a special species.

Most count **geometrical figure** (*shakl*) as a quality: it is the **disposition arising from the enclosure of a magnitude by one or several boundaries**, not the bounded surface itself, which belongs to quantity. Definitions of circle, triangle or square as surfaces enclosed by one curved line or by three or four straight lines describe **the figured magnitude**, not the formal character of its figure. Nor is figure the arrangement of **parts of a body relative to one another or to external things**, which would make it one of *position* (*waḍʿ*), as in the view attributed to Thābit ibn Qurra and favoured at points by al-Rāzī. The mathematical boundaries are not themselves bodily parts. Some objections about whether **relation** enters the definition depend on mistaking a descriptive definition for a real essential definition. Strictly, figure should be described by the configuration produced by boundaries **of a surface or magnitude**, with lines bounding surfaces and surfaces bounding bodies; whether the direct subject of figure is the bounding surface, the interior body or the boundary itself is further debated.

Some geometers count **angle** as quantity, since it can be divided and compared, defining a plane angle as the part of a surface enclosed by lines meeting at a point. This is too broad unless one specifies the surface **immediately adjoining the point of intersection**. Opponents deny that division belongs to the angle **of itself** rather than to its underlying surface. Moreover doubling an **acute angle** can yield a right or obtuse angle; doubling a right angle forms a straight line and seems to eliminate the original angle; doubling an obtuse angle also passes through an alignment at which its former formal type disappears. Doubling quantitative magnitude, however, should not by itself abolish magnitude. The investigators therefore class angle as a **quality peculiar to quantity**, i.e. the geometric disposition at the meeting of bounding lines. A solid angle analogously concerns the meeting of bounding surfaces. Euclid's descriptions of an angle as the meeting of lines, and its ability to be divided or made equal, are then interpreted as descriptions of **the angled surface**, not the abstract angular disposition itself.

title: Dispositional qualities and how the four classes of quality overlap (I.253)
en:
### Dispositional qualities and how the four classes of quality overlap (I.253)

**“Fourth class: dispositional qualities.”** They are characterized by **intense readiness to undergo** an external effect, i.e. an aptitude for being affected easily or rapidly—for example susceptibility to illness and pliancy. Such a disposition is called **weakness** (*ḍaʿf*) or **non-power** (*lā-quwwa*). Its opposite is strong readiness **to resist or not be affected**, as in robust health, hardness, or resistance to compression, called **power** (*quwwa*). If one sought an encompassing account restricted to these two, one could call it a quality determining which of the two aspects of a subject's **receptivity** is favoured.

But most extend dispositional quality to a **third kind**, intense **readiness to act**, such as physical capacity for wrestling. The shared genus must then include a complete bodily disposition **toward something external** or a bodily principle making the occurrence of an effect especially easy. Two arguments contest the third kind. (1) Wrestling skill depends partly on specialized **knowledge and force**, which belong to psychological qualities, and partly on the **hardness and natural conformation of limbs**, already included under resistance to being acted upon. No new third kind is needed. (2) Heat has strong power to burn; counting that power as a dispositional quality while heat itself is a sensible quality appears to place a single thing in two opposed and essential subdivisions of quality.

The force of both objections depends on whether the four classes—**sensible qualities, psychological states and habits, qualities peculiar to magnitude, and dispositional qualities**—are strictly disjoint **essential genera**. If they are instead partly classified by different **aspects**, the same underlying quality may belong to more than one class: heat as sensible and as a powerful active disposition; an animal capacity as psychological insofar as it belongs to an ensouled body, but dispositional insofar as it facilitates action; colour and figure as perceptible, yet also related to quantitative subjects. This brings **Chapter 3, Quality**, to its conclusion in the available electronic source. The ensuing chapter is on **being-where (*ayn*)**.
