title: Being-where, its four alleged forms, and the first moment of occupancy (I.254–255)
en:
### Being-where, its four alleged forms, and the first moment of occupancy (I.254–255)

**“Fourth chapter: being-where (*ayn*).”** This category is the **relation to place**—a thing's occupying a spatial region (*ḥayyiz*). Philosophers and theologians approach its investigation by different methods. The text omits various early theological subdivisions of little use and begins with the theologians, who call the occurrence of a substance in a region its **spatial state** (*kawn*). Many recognize such a state as a real accident even when they deny other **relational accidents**. They usually divide it into four forms: **conjunction** (*ijtimāʿ*), **separation** (*iftirāq*), **motion** (*ḥaraka*), and **rest** (*sukūn*).

If occupancy is considered **relative to another substance**, then either a third substance could intervene between them, in which case there is **separation**, or not, in which case there is **conjunction**. Mere **possibility** of interposition suffices for separation, since two substances separated by a void have no actual third intermediary. Without reference to another substance, if occupancy follows a different region it is **motion**, and if it follows occupancy of **the same region** it is **rest**. Thus rest is the second occupying of a first region, whereas motion is the first occupying of a second region. The ordinal expressions may be applied only by supposition: a thing eternally at rest may never occupy a second region; a moving thing can cease to exist before a second rest occurs. Why is **leaving the first region** also motion? Because entering the second, viewed relative to the second, is **entrance and motion toward it**, and the very same obtaining, viewed relative to the first, is **departure and motion away**.

Conjunction has one basic form of maximal adjacency, also called **contact** (*mumāssa*) by Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī; separation admits degrees of nearness and remoteness. His identification of touching and adjoining is preferable to the doctrine attributed to al-Ashʿarī and certain Muʿtazilites, which makes touch a distinct event following adjacency. An apparent formulation in the *Mawāqif* misleadingly suggests adjacency is a form of separation. Moreover **the conjunction of two atoms** is not one accident inhering in both: each has its own individual conjunction directed toward the other.

**“But occupancy [without a predecessor].”** The fourfold classification is arguably incomplete. God could create a solitary indivisible substance, with no other substance and **no previous location**. Its first spatial state is neither conjunction nor separation, movement nor rest on the stated definitions. Al-Qāḍī and Abū Hāshim nevertheless call the initial state **rest**, because it is essentially like the second occupancy in the same region, and **remaining there** adds an accidental condition not essential to rest. Abū Isḥāq's description of it as “rest in the category or status of motion” can be interpreted along these lines.

This forces a correction to the allegedly exhaustive definition. Simply calling every occupancy **not preceded by occupancy in another region** rest would include stillness following motion in the wrong class when it too has previously occupied another region. Better: **motion** is an occupancy directly succeeding occupancy in a different region, or a *first* occupancy in a *second* region; **rest** is every occupancy not so connected. This places solitary initial occupancy among rests and distinguishes successively contiguous states in a moving body, lest motion collapse into a chain of rests. Al-Qāḍī instead concedes that the **first occupancy of a new region** is itself rest, and says motion is rest insofar as entrance into a region, though not every rest is motion. An objection appeals to the recognized contrariety of motion and rest; the proposed reply restricts contrariety to **motion out of a region versus resting in it**, not movement *into* a region versus occupancy there. The cogency of this turns on whether both occupancies are really the same intrinsic species.

title: Is motion a collection of rests? A relational classification (I.255–257)
en:
### Is motion a collection of rests? A relational classification (I.255–257)

Al-Āmidī disputes the assertion that the first and second occupancy of the same place must be of one kind merely because both localize the substance there. Their causing a common specification does not establish identity in every essential property: the **first occupancy in the second region** is admitted to be motion because it simultaneously constitutes **leaving the first**. If its second occupancy were intrinsically identical, that too would be motion, contrary to agreement. One may reply that “not previously occupying the same place” is an essential condition of motion; but a similar requirement—**not immediately following an occupancy elsewhere**—can distinguish rest. Hence the appeal to similarity proves no more than its opponents grant.

A discussion in the *Mawāqif* alleges that, if motion is defined by **not having preceded it in the same place** rather than by preceding occupancy elsewhere, it cannot consist of **multiple rests**. But “motion is a sum of rests” means **every constituent of motion is a rest**, not **every rest is a constituent of motion**; confusing the two quantifier directions is an error. A more relevant objection is that the solitary first occupancy at creation would on such a definition count as motion, although it is not composed of successive spatial states. If motion is understood as **two successive occupancies in different regions**, its sum-of-parts interpretation makes more sense, though it remains disputable whether the first and second occupancies of a region are of one kind.

**“The precise account.”** Philosophers, as explained later, use *motion* in two senses: the moving subject's **intermediate state** between starting and ending positions, changing continuously from moment to moment; and the **intellectually imagined extended course** from beginning to end. title: Relative motion; philosophers' definition and the two senses of movement (I.258–259)
en:
### Relative motion; philosophers' definition and the two senses of movement (I.258–259)

The dispute over movement of an inner part turns on whether it occupies **the same extended region as the whole**, its own particular dimensional region, or the surrounding atoms. In the case of a stationary stone surrounded by flowing water, the dispute turns on whether its place is an **assumed spatial extension** that it never leaves, or the inner enclosing surface/material bodies that change around it, as certain philosophers define place. Even on the latter theory, one must ask whether movement requires the **placed thing to leave its place**, or whether **its place departing from it** suffices. If movement could arise through departure of surrounding things, a stone might move at once **to the right and left** as different neighbouring bodies pass in opposite directions—an absurdity rightly rejected by most investigators, although accepted by Abū Isḥāq. The *Mawāqif* incorrectly dismisses the dispute as merely verbal: the contenders are claiming to analyze **what movement and place actually are**, not whimsically assigning new names.

**“The philosophers' method.”** One definition calls motion **a passage from potency to act gradually, little by little rather than all at once**. The difficulty is that “gradual” seems to mean occurring in **time**, time is a measure of motion, and the definition becomes circular. Aristotle's alternative describes motion as **the first perfection (actuality) of what is in potency, insofar as it is in potency** (*kamāl awwal li-mā bi-l-quwwa min ḥaythu huwa bi-l-quwwa*). Here “perfection” means acquiring a state previously lacking. A body able to reach another place possesses (a) a potential to **arrive there** and (b) a potential to **move towards it**. The movement toward is **first actuality**, while arrival is **second actuality**, since actual movement precedes completion of the local change. Motion differs from other perfections because its actuality is precisely the **ongoing tending toward a further attainable end**, leaving something still potential as long as the motion exists. After arrival, there is no remaining motion toward that destination. The qualifier “insofar as potential” excludes bodily perfections—such as its own species-form—which are first actualities of the body **as already actually a body**, not actualizations of that bodily possibility of reaching another place.

One objects that the definition is harder to understand than the motion it allegedly defines. Another objects that **circular motion** has no final endpoint that could produce a second actuality. The reply takes Aristotle's formula as an **explication**, not a logically more evident genus-and-differentia definition. In circular movement, each point one chooses can be considered a **destination** with respect to movement approaching it, and an **arrived-at point** with respect to the attainment of it. These are methodological distinctions, not necessarily an absolutely final endpoint for the circle.

**“The conclusion of this account.”** Philosophers distinguish two senses of movement. First is **the actually occurring state of the moving thing being between origin and terminus** (*al-ḥāla al-mutawassiṭa*), continuously present yet **nonabiding**: earlier and later stages cannot coexist, and the intermediate condition can be subdivided **in consideration** without supposing indivisible atoms of motion. Second is **the extended path of movement imagined as one whole from first position to last** (*al-qaṭʿ*). This complete trajectory has no extramental existence **as a coexistent whole**: before arrival it is not finished, and at arrival the motion has ceased. Its unity is instead constructed by memory or imagination retaining the earlier image while experiencing the later. The first, intermediate sense is real and witnessed in experience. The objection that its past is gone and its future not yet, while a present indivisible instant cannot contain extended motion, assumes that existence requires all temporal parts to coexist **at one instant**. Past movement existed **when it was present**, and future movement can exist **when it comes to be**; it does not follow that neither exists simpliciter.

title: Six conditions of motion; changes in position and magnitude (I.260–261)
en:
### Six conditions of motion; changes in position and magnitude (I.260–261)

**“Third investigation.”** Every motion involves six features: (1) the **starting point** (*mā minhu al-ḥaraka*); (2) the **terminus** (*mā ilayhi*); (3) the **respect or category in which change occurs** (*mā fīhi*, such as place, magnitude, quality or position); (4) the **mover**, its efficient cause (*mā bihi*); (5) the **moving subject**, its material cause (*mā lahu*); and (6) **time**. Motion's relation to time in this list is not time's relation to the motion **measured** in the earlier account. In one context motion is the measure's **subject**, whereas here motion is **measured in and by** time.

Beginning and end may be compared **to their motion**, as relational correlates, or **to one another**, as opposed limits. Their opposition is not necessarily two **privatives**, nor a necessary mutual apprehension: one can conceive a beginning without explicitly conceiving a corresponding end. They can have one underlying entity under different descriptions, as a point on a circular orbit functioning as beginning and end at different instants; or things intrinsically contrary, like black and white; or otherwise opposed by their spatial situation, like the center and circumference; or mere distinct points. The **bounds of a movement** thus have a relational dimension, whereas the things that serve as bounds need not be intrinsically contrary in every case.

**“The category of motion.”** Motion's *mā fīhi* is the highest category within which a body passes **successively** between subordinate kinds or varieties. Al-Fārābī explicitly described **movement in position (*waḍʿ*)**, though some expressions of Avicenna may suggest this was a discovery unique to him. A celestial sphere can **rotate on itself** without leaving the place occupied by the sphere as a whole; its hypothetical parts change their **relations to external things** and hence the *position* of the whole changes gradually. In the outermost sphere, which has no containing body on the Aristotelian definition of place, motion in position is especially important. It does not follow that the whole has locomotion merely because each of its imagined parts changes its location: distributing a predicate to every part does not always assign it to the whole **in the same respect**. But the sphere plainly changes orientation, since **position** is itself a relation of part to part and of parts to external landmarks. In this sense the local motion of the parts underlies **positional movement of the whole**.

**“Third, quantity.”** Classical analysis distinguishes change of **magnitude** from lesser to greater or vice versa. Adding new matter in the organism's natural proportions is **growth** (*numuww*); increase without adding matter, as in the remaining air of a bottle after suction, is **rarefaction** (*takhalkhul*). Removal of living matter in the opposite direction is **wasting** (*dhubūl*); decrease in magnitude without removing matter is **condensation** (*takāthuf*). Philosophers argue rarefaction is intelligible because **prime matter** possesses no magnitude in its own essence and can successively receive smaller or larger dimensions through different preparatory causes. Al-Rāzī objects that it is enough to treat magnitude as an accident distinct from a simple body: an intrinsically uniform subject could also receive differing magnitudes. The response is that, unless it is pure potentiality, a body **might have a naturally fixed magnitude**; mere logical uniformity does not prove an unrestricted ability to become every size. The example of a drop becoming as large as an ocean need not follow from allowing some expansions, since extrinsic forces or natural limits may restrict the range. The aim is to establish **some** rarefaction and condensation, not all imaginable magnitudes.
